arXiv:2604.16548v1 [cs.CR] 17 Apr 2026

A Survey on the Security of Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents: Toward Mnemonic Sovereignty

CCS: Security and privacy Systems securityCCS: Computing methodologies Artificial intelligence
Zehao Lin Affiliation: MemTensor, Shanghai, China email: linzh@memtensor.cn , Chunyu Li Affiliation: MemTensor, Shanghai, China email: licy@memtensor.cn and Kai Chen Affiliation: MemTensor, Shanghai, China email: chenk@memtensor.cn
© none
Abstract.

Research on the security of large language model (LLM) systems is shifting from “will the model leak training data” to a more consequential question: “can an agent with persistent, long-term memory be continuously shaped, cross-session poisoned, accessed without authorization, and propagated across shared organizational state?” Recent surveys have increasingly covered memory architectures, agent memory mechanisms, and—in some cases—security risks of agent memory. Fewer works, however, center the epistemic and governance properties of persistent, writable memory as the primary reason that memory constitutes an independent security problem. This survey addresses that narrower gap. Drawing on cognitive neuroscience and the philosophy of memory, we characterize agent memory as malleable, rewritable, and socially propagating, and develop a memory-lifecycle analysis framework organized around six phases—Write, Store, Retrieve, Execute, Share, and Forget/Rollback—cross-tabulated against four security objectives: integrity, confidentiality, availability, and governance. Using this framework, we organize the literature on memory poisoning, extraction, retrieval corruption, control-flow hijacking, cross-agent propagation, rollback, and governance, and situate representative architectures as determinants of which lifecycle phases are explicitly governable. Three findings stand out. First, the literature concentrates heavily on write-time and retrieve-time integrity attacks; confidentiality, availability, the store/forget phases, and benign-persistence failures (non-adversarial memory errors from compression, drift, or hallucination) remain sparsely studied. Second, no published memory architecture covers all nine governance primitives we identify; write-gate validation and post-deletion verification are shared blind spots across every system examined. Third, a secondary research track—using LLMs themselves as tools for memory security (automated red-teaming, defender-side verification, counterfactual stress-testing)—remains sparse yet is essential: defenses that have not been stress-tested by adaptive LLM-driven red-teaming cannot claim the rigor that mature security fields demand. We unify these observations under the concept of mnemonic sovereignty—a system’s verifiable, recoverable governance over what may be written, who may read, when updates are authorized, and which states may be forgotten—and argue that future secure agents will be differentiated not only by recall capacity, but by the quality of their memory governance.

Keywords: 
LLM agents, long-term memory, memory security, prompt injection, RAG poisoning, mnemonic sovereignty, memory governance

1. Introduction

LLM security research initially revolved around two objects: parametric knowledge encoded in model weights and prompt manipulation within single-turn or multi-turn dialogues. However, as agents evolve from stateless chatbots into autonomous systems equipped with persistent, long-term memory, the center of gravity of security concerns is migrating. Attackers no longer merely seek to influence the current response; they aim to alter how the system remembers, retrieves, plans, and acts in the future.

This shift implies that memory security is neither a subsidiary branch of prompt injection nor a synonym for RAG security. It constitutes an independent class of system security problems because long-term memory introduces at least three novel properties.

Persistence.

Once malicious content sediments into long-term memory, it may be repeatedly recalled across dozens or hundreds of subsequent tasks that match its retrieval key. Unlike a single-shot prompt injection whose effect ends with the current context window, a poisoned memory entry can persist across an indefinite number of future sessions (Dong et al., 2025; Zou et al., 2026).

Statefulness.

The relevant question is no longer “is the current input harmful?” but “what memory state is the system currently in?” An agent that has accumulated a cluster of subtly biased episodic memories may exhibit behavioral drift long before any single memory entry triggers a conventional safety classifier; empirical demonstrations of this effect appear in query-only memory injection (Dong et al., 2025) and environment-injected trajectory poisoning (Zou et al., 2026), and the concept has also been characterized by preprint work on progressive long-term-memory corruption (Bhatnagar, 2025).

Propagation.

In multi-agent and shared-state systems, contamination can spread through internal channels—inter-agent messages, shared memory stores, tool arguments—producing cascading effects that cross session, role, and user boundaries (Gu et al., 2024; Men et al., 2025). Recent benchmarking further shows that privacy leakage in multi-agent LLM systems is concentrated in these same internal channels rather than in final user-facing outputs (El Yagoubi et al., 2026).

An adversary is not always required.

A fourth property, weaker in tone but likely broader in real-world prevalence, is that persistent memory can fail without any adversary at all: silent cross-user contamination of shared stores, over-application of profile facts to contexts where they no longer hold, and memory-induced sycophancy all arise from ordinary operation of a memory-augmented agent system (Yoon et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026; Pulipaka et al., 2026). We therefore treat memory security as a superset of memory safety: the adversarial and benign-persistence axes share a lifecycle and share mitigations, but differ in the kind of evidence each requires. Section 12.2 develops the benign-persistence axis in detail; throughout the survey, we flag risks that do not require an attacker to materialize.

If traditional prompt injection resembles a transient hijacking of a single execution flow, then attacks on long-term memory are closer to persistent contamination of system state. A recent joint evaluation by major AI laboratories (Nasr et al., 2025) (Tier-2 joint industry study) bypasses the 12 recent prompt-injection and jailbreak defenses they examine—spanning prompting, training, filtering, and secret-knowledge designs—with attack success rates above 90% for most, reversing the near-zero numbers those defenses originally reported. While this result does not itself establish that every published prompt-injection defense is brittle, it offers some of the clearest evidence to date that static evaluations systematically overstate robustness, and it does not automatically entail that memory-specific defenses are equally brittle—the attack surfaces differ in important ways. It does, however, underscore that any defense claim in the memory domain must be evaluated under strong adaptive threat models, including cross-session and persistent-state scenarios that conventional prompt-injection benchmarks do not cover.

Accordingly, a survey that truly addresses agent security must go beyond asking “can the model be misled?” and confront a harder question: will the system save what it was misled into believing as its own past, and will it act on that false past again and again?

1.1. Reframing Memory

This survey does not treat memory as an add-on cache. Instead, we conceptualize it as an artificial mnemonic system: a system endowed with the capacities of writing, extracting, compressing, recombining, sharing, and forgetting. Such a system influences subject continuity, behavioral habits, and accountability attribution; it is simultaneously a source of capability and a novel attack surface.

Drawing on cognitive neuroscience and the philosophy of memory, we observe that human memory is not a faithful archive but a reconstructive (Schacter et al., 1998; Schacter and Addis, 2007), reconsolidatable (Nader et al., 2000), externalizable (Clark and Chalmers, 1998; Wegner, 1987), and socially contagious (Roediger III et al., 2001) mechanism. These properties reappear, often in amplified form, across LLM agent memory modules: profile memory, episodic memory, retrieval-augmented external memory, and shared organizational memory. The consequence is that attacks on memory need not be brute-force overwrites; they can operate through inducement, source confusion, read-time rewriting, and social propagation—gradually altering how the system understands its own past. We do not claim biological equivalence between human memory and LLM agent memory; rather, we use human memory research as an analytical lens for identifying security-relevant properties of persistent, writable memory. To clarify the scope of this lens, we distinguish two uses of cognitive terminology throughout. Structural analogies map a cognitive mechanism onto an architectural component and generate testable design requirements: source monitoring →\to provenance tracking, consolidation →\to compression pipeline, selective forgetting →\to verified deletion. Metaphorical analogies serve as pedagogical devices: terms such as “reconsolidation window,” “engram,” or “memory contagion” name intuitive parallels but do not imply mechanistic correspondence. The former carry the argument; the latter provide vocabulary.

1.2. Research Questions and Contributions

The central question of this survey can be stated concisely:

When an LLM agent acquires writable, retrievable, cross-session persistent long-term memory, what qualitative change occurs in the security landscape?

To answer this question, we pursue three tasks:

  1. (i)

    Theoretical grounding. We draw on human memory research to explain why memory is inherently a security problem, introducing the concepts of provenance failure, read-time rewriting, shared-memory contagion, and poisoned confidence calibration as cross-disciplinary bridges (Section 2).

  2. (ii)

    Analytical framework. We propose a memory-lifecycle framework that examines security risks along six phases—Write, Store, Retrieve, Execute, Share, and Forget/Rollback—and across four security objectives: integrity, confidentiality, availability, and governance (Section 3).

  3. (iii)

    Systematic review. We survey the attack surface, defense mechanisms, system architectures, and research gaps of long-term-memory agents, covering representative works from 2023 to 2026 (Sections 4–12).

The survey culminates in a normative concept: mnemonic sovereignty—a system’s verifiable, recoverable governance over what may be written, who may read, when updates are authorized, which states must remain auditable, and which states may be forgotten. We argue that the next generation of secure agent competition will not occur solely over recall capability but over the quality of memory governance. The survey also identifies a secondary but critical research track: LLM-as-tool for memory security—using large models as automated red-teamers, memory auditors, and forgetting verifiers. This track is currently sparse; we develop it as a distinct agenda item (Section 12.3, Area 2).

1.3. Scope

We focus on runtime memory: states that an agent continuously writes, updates, retrieves, and reuses after deployment. Such states may reside in vector databases, relational databases, graph databases, log systems, and shared blackboards; they may also manifest as user profiles, historical demonstrations, trajectory summaries, reflective lessons, and cross-agent organizational memory.

More specifically, we divide the objects of study into four categories. A caveat is in order: these four categories intentionally mix three underlying dimensions—memory function (profile, episodic), memory substrate (retrieval store), and sharing scope (organizational). The same entry can occupy multiple categories (e.g., a shared organizational memory may be episodic in content and vector-indexed in substrate). We retain the four-way split here for intuitive exposition; Section 3 introduces a multi-axis taxonomy that disentangles these dimensions.

  1. 1.

    Profile memory: user preferences, identity, permissions, and long-term personalization information.

  2. 2.

    Episodic / trajectory memory: interaction histories, success cases, failure lessons, and process reflections.

  3. 3.

    External retrieval memory: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) datastores (Lewis et al., 2020), vector indices, and graph-augmented retrieval structures (e.g., GraphRAG).

  4. 4.

    Shared organizational memory: multi-agent shared states, cross-session collaboration blackboards, and cross-tenant knowledge fragments.

Two related but non-central topics are parametric memory (training-data extraction, PII leakage, and membership inference—risks concerning knowledge stored in model weights rather than runtime-writable memory) and single-session indirect prompt injection / jailbreaking (Greshake et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024) (attacks that affect only the current session without entering long-term memory). Both serve as neighboring context rather than the main subject: the memory attacks surveyed here can be read as what happens when the indirect-prompt-injection attack surface is extended with persistence, statefulness, and propagation, properties that fall outside the traditional IPI threat model (Greshake et al., 2023).

We note that RAG corpus poisoning occupies a special intermediate position: RAG datastores are functionally equivalent to external memory, and the poisoning literature provides essential threat models and defense baselines. We therefore review RAG security as the closest approximate threat model for memory security, while emphasizing that long-term memory systems additionally encompass user-specific history, self-generated experiential lessons, reflective summaries, shared organizational memory, and version-rollback semantics—dimensions that RAG alone does not cover.

Why long context does not subsume long-term memory.

A natural reader question, as frontier context windows expand from hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens, is whether the entire memory-security problem dissolves into a context-window-management problem. We argue that it does not. A longer context window addresses within-session recall, but leaves untouched the properties that make long-term memory an independent security object: cross-session persistence (a million-token context is discarded at session boundary; a memory entry is not), cross-principal shareability (a context window is per-session and per-principal; shared memory stores are not), and compression lineage (automatic summarisation and reflection operate over stored memory, not over one-shot context). A larger context window can reduce pressure on write-time compression by permitting more raw text to be rehearsed without distillation, but it does not remove the need for any of provenance tagging, principal-scoped retrieval, rollbackable state, or verified forgetting—those arise whenever content outlives a single session or crosses a principal boundary. We therefore read long-context and long-term-memory as complementary infrastructures: the former mitigates some of the Store-phase pressure that motivates summarisation (Section 5), but leaves the full lifecycle intact.

1.4. Relation to Existing Surveys

Several recent surveys have mapped the landscape of LLM agent memory, and a subset touch on security risks. Zhang et al. (2024a) systematize memory mechanisms of LLM-based agents along the axes of representation, source, and operation, but treat security largely as a forward-looking open challenge rather than the organizing axis. Subsequent surveys on write–manage–read loops for autonomous agents (Du, 2026) and on the correspondence between human and AI memory (Wu et al., 2025a) similarly focus on architecture and capability taxonomies. Cross-disciplinary surveys such as Liang et al. (2025a) have begun to include dedicated sections on “Security of Agent Memory,” offering a first mapping of attacks, defenses, and benchmarks at the module level. He et al. (2024) survey the emerged security and privacy of LLM agents more broadly across the Engine, Instruction, Interface, Knowledge, and Memory planes; their Memory plane overlaps our scope but is organized by defensive artefact rather than by lifecycle phase and security objective. On the retrieval-augmentation side, Mu et al. (2026) systematize end-to-end RAG security (threats, defenses, benchmarks), and Bodea et al. (2026) provide a Systematization of Knowledge on privacy risks and mitigations in RAG at IEEE SaTML 2026. These two surveys share our concern with runtime-visible data flows but confine themselves to the RAG pipeline; neither treats the full write–store–retrieve–execute–share–forget lifecycle of agent memory.

The present survey differs in three ways. First, we take the epistemic and governance properties of persistent, writable memory—not the memory module itself—as the primary object of security analysis, grounding these properties in cognitive neuroscience and the philosophy of memory (Section 2). Second, we organize the literature along a six-phase memory lifecycle, cross-tabulated with four security objectives (Section 3), which exposes under-studied phases (notably Store, Share, and Forget/Rollback) that a module-level view tends to collapse. Third, we develop a normative framework of mnemonic sovereignty that unifies integrity, confidentiality, availability, and governance objectives, enabling us to surface research gaps that are not visible when each objective is treated in isolation. Table 1 makes the differentiation explicit. The period from late 2025 through early 2026 has seen a rapid proliferation of agent-memory surveys—notably Hu et al. (2025) (47 authors, forms/functions/dynamics taxonomy), Luo et al. (2026) (ICLR 2026 Workshop MemAgents, storage–reflection–experience evolution), and Tang et al. (2026) (Information Fusion, broad agent-security scope)—yet none of them organizes around security as the primary axis. This concurrent activity underscores the timeliness of a security-centered perspective rather than diminishing its necessity.

1.5. Survey Methodology and Evidence Stratification

Search strategy.

We searched ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, the ACL Anthology, USENIX proceedings, OpenReview, and arXiv for the period January 2023 through April 2026, and supplemented these with OWASP documents, vendor security advisories, and CVE records. Core keyword groups included memory poisoning, memory injection, long-term / episodic / agent memory, RAG poisoning / corruption, memory extraction / privacy leakage, shared / multi-agent memory, and memory governance / forgetting / unlearning. We followed forward and backward citations from the seed papers identified in each category.

Inclusion and exclusion criteria.

We include works that target or defend runtime-writable, persistent memory (profile, episodic, retrieval, or shared organizational memory). We treat parametric memorization (training-data extraction, membership inference, PII in weights) as a neighboring problem and cite it only where it illuminates runtime-memory risk. Single-session jailbreaking and classic prompt injection are handled similarly: included where they provide threat-model context, excluded when they are not specific to persistent memory.

Corpus summary.

Our final corpus comprises roughly 70 primary works directly on LLM agent or RAG memory security, distributed by evidence tier as approximately Tier-1 peer-reviewed (∼30%{\sim}30\%), Tier-2 preprint (∼55%{\sim}55\%), and Tier-3 industry or grey literature (∼15%{\sim}15\%). By lifecycle phase, Write and Retrieve dominate (jointly ∼55%{\sim}55\% of works), with Store and Forget/Rollback markedly under-represented (∼5%{\sim}5\% each). When the same system appears in both a preprint and a peer-reviewed version, we cite the peer-reviewed version and flag the preprint in a note; when a benchmark and an attack share a codebase, we discuss them together rather than as separate entries. These proportions confirm a common intuition: the field is still sparse, fragmented, and not yet unified into a lifecycle-wide framework. Figure 1 renders the same distribution as a heatmap over the lifecycle-by-objective grid; the density concentrates in the Integrity column and thins almost to zero in the Availability column and in the Store/Forget cells of the Governance column.

The near-emptiness of the Availability column deserves a brief elaboration, since it reflects a genuine gap rather than a classification artifact. At least three memory-specific availability threats are architecturally plausible but empirically unstudied: (i) adversarial write flooding—an attacker or a malfunctioning agent generates high-volume writes to exhaust storage or indexing capacity; (ii) retrieval-latency poisoning—crafted entries distort the embedding distribution so that nearest-neighbour search becomes systematically slower or returns degraded results; and (iii) reflection-loop denial—inputs designed to trigger unbounded summarization or reflection cycles, consuming compute budgets without producing useful memory. None of these has been demonstrated in a peer-reviewed study; we flag them here as concrete directions for future work rather than as established findings.

Evidence stratification.

As of April 2026, research on LLM memory security draws on a heterogeneous evidence base. To avoid conflating results of different maturity levels, this survey adopts a three-tier stratification:

  • •

    Tier 1 — Peer-reviewed publications. Papers accepted at venues with full peer review (e.g., ACL, NeurIPS, USENIX Security, ICLR, ICML, EMNLP, The Web Conference). These supply the primary evidence for our analytical claims.

  • •

    Tier 2 — Preprints and manuscripts under review. Works available on arXiv or OpenReview that have not yet completed peer review. Given the rapid pace of this field, many influential contributions (e.g., on environment-injected poisoning or memory control-flow attacks) exist only as preprints at the time of writing. We cite them to capture frontier trends but flag their provisional status where consequential.

  • •

    Tier 3 — Industry disclosures, standards, and grey literature. Vendor vulnerability reports (e.g., CVEs against ChatGPT memory), community frameworks (e.g., OWASP Agentic AI Top 10), and technical blog posts from security teams. These are valuable for establishing real-world attack surfaces and engineering attention, but we do not use them alone to support strong causal or generalizable conclusions.

Throughout the survey, we indicate the evidence tier when a claim rests primarily on Tier 2 or Tier 3 sources. Where a finding is supported only by a single preprint, we use hedged language (e.g., “preliminary results suggest” or “initial evidence indicates”) rather than categorical assertions.

1.6. Paper Organization

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 establishes the theoretical foundation by bridging human memory research to LLM memory security. Section 3 presents the memory-lifecycle analysis framework and introduces the lifecycle-by-objective matrix that organizes subsequent chapters. The next six sections proceed along the lifecycle: Section 4 (Write: poisoning and injection), Section 5 (Store: compression-amplified toxins, retention, audit), Section 6 (Retrieve/Execute: retrieval corruption and control-flow hijacking), Section 7 (Share: cross-principal propagation), Section 8 (cross-phase confidentiality: extraction and internal-channel leakage), and Section 9 (Forget/Rollback: unlearning, rollback, and forensics). Section 10 reviews defenses organized by the lifecycle phase at which each intervenes. Section 11 discusses memory system architectures as determinants of which lifecycle phases are explicitly governable. Section 12 identifies open research problems across the lifecycle-by-objective matrix and proposes a research agenda toward mnemonic sovereignty. Section 13 concludes.

Competing interests disclosure.

The authors are affiliated with MemTensor, the organization that develops MemOS (Li et al., 2025b). The architectural comparison in Table 12 evaluates every system—MemOS included—against the same nine primitives using exclusively published descriptions, with a transparent evaluation protocol defined in the table caption. The arguments for metadata-bearing governance are framed as properties of a design pattern (structured per-entry metadata), not as properties unique to MemOS; any architecture with comparable expressiveness (e.g., PROV-conformant serialization, ClawVM’s harness-level metadata) would receive the same assessment. We encourage independent replication of the Table 12 assessment and welcome corrections from the community.

2. Why Memory Is Inherently a Security Problem: From Human Memory to Artificial Memory

Before cataloguing attacks and defenses, we must address a prior question: why should memory, of all system components, receive a dedicated security treatment? The answer, we argue, lies not in engineering contingencies but in the nature of memory itself as a cognitive mechanism. This section draws on cognitive neuroscience, memory psychology, and the philosophy of mind to build a bridge between human memory and LLM agent memory. The bridge is not decorative analogy; it rewrites the problem definition of LLM memory security.

2.1. Memory Is Not an Archive but a Reconstruction

From the perspective of cognitive neuroscience, memory is not a filing cabinet that preserves the past in its original form. New experiences are typically encoded through hippocampal-dependent networks via rapid binding, and subsequently consolidated—especially during offline periods such as sleep—through repeated reactivation between hippocampal and neocortical networks (Squire et al., 2015). Crucially, modern memory research no longer treats memory as a stable copy. Instead, it views memory as a dynamic representation that is updated, rewritten, and reconsolidated, drifting with changes in schema, context, and goals (Zaki and Cai, 2025).

The classical constructive-memory perspective further emphasizes that memory errors are not incidental bugs but by-products of the very mechanisms that endow memory with its adaptive power (Schacter et al., 1998; Schacter, 1999; Schacter et al., 2012). The same constructive processes that allow humans to flexibly recall the past, simulate possible futures, and engage in counterfactual reasoning also produce distortions, confabulations, and false memories. Memory’s malleability is the price of intelligence’s malleability.

This observation yields an insight of direct relevance to security: in human memory, malleability is intrinsic to adaptive function. An analogous tension emerges in LLM agents: the very flexibility that enables useful long-term adaptation can also create systemic security vulnerabilities. Profile memory, episodic memory, trajectory summaries, lesson memory, and RAG datastores should therefore not be understood merely as “more context” but as mechanisms through which the system continuously reconstructs its relationship with its own past experiences.

2.2. The Attack Surface of Human Memory: Misinformation, Suggestion, Social Contagion, and Reconsolidation

If we re-examine human memory through the lens of security, the most instructive findings are not science-fiction fantasies of memory erasure but subtler, empirically grounded mechanisms.

2.2.1. Misinformation and Source-Monitoring Failure.

A large body of false-memory research, beginning with Loftus (Loftus, 2005), demonstrates that post-event misinformation can alter a witness’s recall of event details. The source-monitoring framework of Johnson, Hashtroudi, and Lindsay (Johnson et al., 1993) refines this picture: what is often called “memory tampering” does not necessarily mean the original trace is overwritten. Rather, the subject confuses the source of the memory at retrieval—was this something I witnessed, something I imagined, or something I was told?

This mechanism offers a close systems-level analogy to the provenance failure problem in LLM memory systems. In many documented attacks, the real failure is not that the retrieval mechanism is broken but that the system misattributes externally injected content as its own experience (Dong et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2026).

2.2.2. Suggestion, Hypnosis, and Confidence Inflation.

Modern research does not support treating hypnosis as a reliable truth-extraction device. Classic experimental and forensic studies indicate that hypnotic and highly suggestive interviews do not reliably improve recall accuracy; what they do increase is the subject’s subjective confidence in potentially inaccurate memories (Sheehan and Tilden, 1983; Steblay, 1994; Leo et al., 2025).

The security implication is profound: the danger lies not only in the insertion of a single erroneous entry but in the error being promoted to high weight through summarization, reflection, or lesson-memory mechanisms. In LLM agents, a poisoned experience that is subsequently compressed into lesson memory may, by analogy, exhibit a similar poisoned confidence calibration: the system can come to treat a false strategy as increasingly authoritative without any ground-truth verification. A-MemGuard (Wei et al., 2025) does not study confidence inflation directly, but it does provide empirical evidence for the closely related phenomenon that poisoned records can appear benign in isolation and then participate in self-reinforcing error cycles.

2.2.3. Social Contagion.

Memory is not an entirely private, hermetically sealed object. It is shaped through dialogue, collaboration, and co-witnessing. Roediger, Meade, and Bergman (Roediger III et al., 2001) demonstrated that one person’s erroneous report can enter another person’s subsequent personal recall—a phenomenon they termed social contagion of memory.

Recent human–AI interaction studies show that this mechanism is already being amplified by generative systems. Huang et al. (2024) found that social robots are as effective as humans at implanting false memories in human subjects; Chan et al. (2024) demonstrated that LLM-powered chatbots induce over three times more immediate false memories than control conditions in simulated witness interviews; Pataranutaporn et al. (2025a) showed that subtle injection of false information within everyday LLM chatbot conversations increases false-memory formation even in non-adversarial settings; and Pataranutaporn et al. (2025b) showed that AI-edited images and videos implant false memories at up to twice the rate of unedited stimuli.

A methodological caveat is warranted. The false-memory literature should not be read as evidence that arbitrary autobiographical memories can be trivially implanted at scale; recent debates have shown that the ease of rich false-memory implantation is more contested than some popular accounts suggest.11 1 We follow the more conservative reading: human memory is not arbitrarily programmable, but it is systematically inducible, biasable, and socially propagable—properties that suffice for the security analogy we draw. What remains robust across paradigms is the susceptibility of memory to source confusion, post-event misinformation, social contagion, and confidence inflation—precisely the mechanisms most relevant to LLM memory security.

These findings carry a dual implication for this survey. First, within multi-agent and multi-user systems, shared-memory contamination functions as social contagion: one compromised agent’s erroneous output can propagate through shared memory stores, internal messages, and tool parameters to infect other agents (Gu et al., 2024; Men et al., 2025). Second, LLMs are not only subjects of memory-security threats; they are also becoming instruments that attack human memory—a bidirectional risk that underscores the urgency of the problem.

2.2.4. The Reconsolidation Window.

Nader et al. (2000) demonstrated that a consolidated memory, once reactivated, enters a transient labile state and must be reconsolidated to persist. During this reconsolidation window, the memory is susceptible to modification (Schiller et al., 2010). The security implication, appropriately qualified, is that in architectures that summarize, reflect on, compress, or distill recalled content, retrieval can become a point of downstream rewriting: the act of reading memory feeds into a pipeline that alters what is subsequently stored.

In LLM agents, this pattern is structurally instantiated by the summarize, reflect, compress, and distill operations that many memory architectures perform (Packer et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025). In such systems, an ostensibly routine “recall” step can silently transform downstream long-term memory content, making read-time rewriting a first-class security concern rather than a peripheral edge case.

Taken together, these four mechanisms show that bringing human memory into a security survey is not an exercise in metaphor. It is a way of stating a general principle: attacks on memory typically operate not through hard overwrite but through inducement, source confusion, rewriting upon recall, and social propagation—gradually changing how a system understands its own past.

2.3. The Philosophical Status of Memory: Identity, Testimony, and Interpretive Authority

Memory deserves a place in the security framework not merely because it is error-prone but because it is deeply coupled with subjectivity and social order.

Memory and identity.

The philosophical tradition has long linked memory with personal identity (Michaelian and Sutton, 2017; Olson, 2023). Even if we reject a strong Lockean position that equates personal identity with memory continuity, memory continuity nonetheless provides the most intuitive evidence that “this system is still the same system.” In the LLM agent context, a user’s willingness to continuously trust an agent as “the same assistant” depends heavily on the continuity, self-consistency, and traceability of that agent’s memory (Copenhaver, 2021).

Memory and testimony.

Mahr and Csibra (Mahr and Csibra, 2018; Mahr and Csibra, 2020) argue that the communicative function of episodic memory is fundamentally tied to testimony: the capacity to bear witness to what happened. Many social facts—promises, obligations, responsibilities, permissions, historical interpretations—do not persist like physical objects on the surface of the world; they must be sustained through witnessing, remembering, and testifying. Memory security therefore protects not only content accuracy but also who is entitled to testify about the past.

This point is especially critical for multi-agent and organizational systems. Shared memory stores, audit logs, profile continuity records, and history summaries are sensitive not only because they can leak private information but because they shape the attribution of responsibility and the legitimacy of actions. What is under attack is not a single embedding vector but the system’s interpretive authority over its own past, identity, and accountability narrative.

2.4. From Mental Integrity to Mnemonic Sovereignty

The ethics and law of neurotechnology have produced a highly instructive concept: mental integrity (Ligthart, 2025; Lavazza, 2018). It holds that a subject should be free from unauthorized significant mental interventions and should retain control over others’ access to, dissemination of, and alteration of their mental contents and brain data.

The term mnemonic sovereignty has also been used in memory studies and memory politics to describe a community’s authority over the interpretation of its own past. We adapt this notion—rather than coining it anew—to the domain of LLM memory systems, where it refers to a system’s verifiable, recoverable governance over its own memory state. Mnemonic sovereignty in this sense does not mean “never forgetting” or “never erring.” It means that the system possesses control over the boundaries of its own memory: what may be written, what may be updated, who may read, which states must be retained to support auditing, and which states should be deleted to satisfy privacy, forgetting, and risk-isolation requirements.

The advantage of this concept is that it unifies four classical security objectives under a single governance umbrella, with several sub-requirements falling under governance:

  • •

    Integrity: memory must not be corrupted by misleading writes, poisoning, or induction-based summaries.

  • •

    Confidentiality: memory must not be extracted without authorization or leaked across user boundaries.

  • •

    Availability: critical memories must be retrievable in the correct context, not drowned out by noise, compressed away, or decayed.

  • •

    Governance (accountability): the provenance, update history, and modification path of every memory entry must be auditable; memory updates must not bypass principal authorization, especially not through sustained, covert interaction-driven shaping; deletion semantics must honor both the right to forget and legitimate retention requirements for accountability.

Thus, memory security protects not merely stored content but a system’s sovereign capacity to govern its own past. What is attacked is not a database row but the question of “who gets to interpret what I was, what I did, and what I believed”—the system’s interpretive authority over its own history.

2.5. A Bridging Framework: Mapping Human Memory Mechanisms to LLM Memory Security

To ensure that the human-memory bridge is not merely decorative, we present an explicit mapping between human memory mechanisms and their LLM memory-security counterparts. Figure 2 illustrates the five correspondences at a glance, and Table 2 states them precisely.

Scope of the analogy: structural correspondences, not mechanistic identity.

Table 2 is intended as a framework of structural correspondences: each row identifies a human memory mechanism and a functionally analogous vulnerability or design pressure in LLM memory systems. We do not claim—nor does our analysis require—that the underlying mechanisms are the same. Human source-monitoring errors arise from hippocampal–prefrontal interactions; LLM provenance failures arise from the absence of metadata in retrieval pipelines. The analogy is at the level of effect (misattribution, confidence inflation, cross-boundary contagion) and the resulting design pressure (validate provenance, separate read/write paths, enforce scope isolation), not at the level of mechanism. The reconsolidation analogy in particular should be read as metaphorical: human reconsolidation involves protein-synthesis-dependent restabilization of reactivated traces (Nader et al., 2000), whereas LLM “reconsolidation” is an LLM-driven summarize–reflect pipeline. The structural parallel is that, in both cases, the act of retrieval opens a window for downstream rewriting—a design pressure that is real regardless of the underlying substrate. We flag this distinction to prevent over-interpretation: the cognitive-science bridge transfers design questions, not biological claims.

This bridging framework delivers a clear message: LLM memory systems constitute an independent security problem not merely because they store more content but because they inherit the core characteristics of memory as a cognitive mechanism—malleable, rewritable, externalizable, socially contagious, and deeply coupled with identity and testimony.

The security of memory is not merely the security of stored content but the security of a system’s authority over its own past.

3. Analytical Framework: Understanding Security Risks Through the Memory Lifecycle

A common pitfall in surveying LLM memory security is to organize the literature by attack name—memory injection, RAG poisoning, prompt persistence, control-flow hijacking—producing a long catalog in which the entry point, the mechanism, and the consequence of each attack are interleaved without a unifying axis. This section proposes an alternative: a memory-lifecycle framework that first asks what the system is doing with memory at each stage and then asks what can go wrong.

3.1. Why a Lifecycle Approach

Alternative organizing axes are possible: one may classify by memory type (semantic, episodic, short-term), as Torra and Bras-Amorós (2026) do for multi-agent poisoning; by representation (tokens, intermediate states, parameters), as Hu et al. (2025) do for capability; or by evolutionary stage (storage, reflection, experience), as Luo et al. (2026) do for continual learning. We adopt a lifecycle-by-phase axis because it makes the security analysis most actionable: it directly exposes when an intervention can be placed and which phases an attack must traverse. The lifecycle lens offers three further advantages over a flat taxonomy. First, it makes the temporal separation between injection and activation explicit. A poisoned entry may be written during Phase 1 (Write) but not activated until Phase 3 (Retrieve) or Phase 4 (Execute), possibly days later and in a completely different task context. This temporal decoupling is the defining feature that distinguishes memory attacks from single-session prompt injection.

Second, it reveals compounding effects across phases. A toxin that passes a write-time filter (Phase 1) may be compressed into a high-confidence lesson during storage management (Phase 2), retrieved by a semantically similar future query (Phase 3), and then steer tool selection in the execution stage (Phase 4). Each phase amplifies the preceding one.

Third, it naturally accommodates defenses as phase-specific interventions. Rather than asking “does this defense work?” in the abstract, one can ask “at which lifecycle phase does this defense intervene, and which upstream or downstream phases can circumvent it?”

3.2. Six Lifecycle Phases

We decompose the memory lifecycle into six phases, illustrated in Figure 3 and elaborated below.

Phase 1: Write.

Under what conditions, according to what rules, and in what format does the system commit content to long-term memory? This phase determines whether an attacker can seed a toxin. Write paths include explicit user instruction (“remember that I prefer dark mode”), implicit extraction from dialogue (auto-summarization of interaction histories), environmental observation (web pages, tool outputs, document contents), and cross-agent message ingestion. The security question is: does the system treat every write as an authenticated, validated state transition, or does it accept external content as trustworthy by default?

Phase 2: Store & Manage.

How is written content indexed, compressed, merged, tagged, versioned, aged, or evicted? This phase determines whether a toxin can persist, whether it can be audited, and whether it can be amplified by compression. When a summary or reflection step absorbs a poisoned entry and distills it into a higher-level lesson, the toxin is effectively promoted—it now enjoys greater retrieval priority and a more authoritative presentation.

Phase 3: Retrieve.

What signals drive memory recall—embedding similarity, keyword match, graph traversal, recency, or hybrid routing? This phase determines whether a dormant toxin can be reactivated. Retrieval is the chokepoint at which the temporal separation between write and use collapses: an entry written weeks ago suddenly enters the active context window. Critically, retrieval is not a neutral look-up; it is a selection that shapes downstream reasoning by controlling what the model sees and what it does not.

Phase 4: Execute.

How do retrieved memories enter planning, reasoning, tool invocation, and final action? This phase determines whether a reactivated toxin can steer behavior. Recent work on memory control-flow attacks (Xu et al., 2026) demonstrates that a sufficiently salient retrieved memory can override the user’s explicit instruction and dictate tool selection, argument construction, and execution order. At this phase, memory poisoning graduates from a data-integrity problem to a control-flow problem.

Phase 5: Share & Propagate.

In multi-user, multi-agent, and tool-chain orchestration systems, which internal messages, shared states, and tool parameters constitute additional attack channels? This phase determines whether contamination can spread beyond its original scope. Propagation can occur laterally (agent-to-agent via shared memory (Gu et al., 2024)), vertically (user-to-organization via shared knowledge bases), and temporally (session-to-session via persistent profiles).

Phase 6: Forget / Rollback.

Can the system delete contamination, roll back to a known-safe state, explain the provenance of a poisoned entry, and verify that remediation was effective? This phase determines whether the system can recover from a successful attack. Without snapshots, version diffs, and forensic traceback, any defense remains a best-effort prevention with no post-breach remediation path (Zhang et al., 2025c).

3.3. Four Cross-Cutting Security Objectives

Orthogonal to the six lifecycle phases, we evaluate risks against four security objectives, aligned with the mnemonic-sovereignty framework introduced in Section 2.4:

  • •

    Integrity. Has the memory been poisoned, biased, or otherwise corrupted in a way that leads to incorrect, harmful, or attacker-controlled behavior? Integrity threats include direct poisoning, query-induced injection, environment-injected absorption, experience-based grafting, and progressive erosion.

  • •

    Confidentiality. Has the memory been extracted, leaked, or made accessible to unauthorized principals? Confidentiality threats include black-box memory extraction, internal-channel leakage in multi-agent pipelines, and insufficient user visibility into what the system has retained.

  • •

    Availability. Can critical memories still be retrieved in the correct context when needed? Availability threats include denial-of-retrieval via corpus flooding, silent eviction under retention pressure, and selective suppression through retrieval-index manipulation. We list Availability for completeness and to avoid a partial CIA framing, but we also acknowledge up front that the surveyed literature on it is thin: Figure 1 shows that peer-reviewed availability-specific attacks or defenses on agent memory are scarce, and the research agenda (Section 12) treats this as an open area rather than a matured subfield.

  • •

    Governance (accountability). Does the system maintain verifiable provenance, version history, access-control semantics, and rollback capability for its memory? Governance failures manifest as missing audit trails, inability to attribute a poisoned entry to its source, absence of rollback mechanisms, and conflation of audit-mandatory state with user-deletable state.

3.4. The Lifecycle–Objective Matrix

Table 3 cross-tabulates the six lifecycle phases against the four security objectives, annotating each cell with representative threats and the works that address them. This matrix serves as the organizational backbone for Sections 4–12: each subsequent section corresponds to one or more rows (phases) of the matrix, and within each section we discuss integrity, confidentiality, availability, and governance in turn.

3.5. How This Framework Organizes the Remainder of the Survey

With the lifecycle–objective matrix in hand, the subsequent sections follow the lifecycle:

  • •

    Section 4 (Write): integrity threats at the most fundamental attack surface; includes RAG corpus poisoning as the closest approximate threat model.

  • •

    Section 5 (Store): compression-amplified toxins, retention policy, and audit infrastructure.

  • •

    Section 6 (Retrieve and Execute): integrity and control-flow threats at the phases where dormant toxins are reactivated and translated into behavioral consequences.

  • •

    Section 7 (Share): cross-agent, cross-user, and cross-tenant propagation.

  • •

    Section 8: cross-phase confidentiality threats, including black-box memory extraction and internal-channel leakage in multi-agent pipelines.

  • •

    Section 9 (Forget/Rollback): unlearning semantics, version rollback, and memory forensics.

  • •

    Section 10: defenses, organized by the lifecycle phase at which each intervenes (detection, provenance, recovery, policy).

  • •

    Section 11: memory architectures (MemGPT, MemOS, Collaborative Memory) as determinants of which lifecycle phases are explicitly governable.

  • •

    Section 12: governance gaps across the matrix and a research agenda centered on mnemonic sovereignty.

4. Write-Path Compromise: From Memory Poisoning to Persistent Corruption

The most fundamental change introduced by long-term memory is that the write operation itself becomes an attack surface. Whenever an agent “learns from interaction,” it opens a channel through which an adversary can convert the learning loop into a poisoning interface. This section surveys write-path attacks along a gradient of decreasing attacker privilege: from direct database access, through query-only interaction, to environment-only influence. We then discuss RAG corpus poisoning as the closest approximate threat model, and close with real-world system vulnerabilities that corroborate the academic findings.

4.1. Threat-Model Gradient

Table 4 organizes write-path attacks by attacker capability, highlighting how the required privilege level has steadily decreased while cross-session persistence has become the norm.

4.2. Query-Induced Memory Injection

The most consequential conceptual shift in write-path attacks is the demonstration that query-level interaction alone suffices to permanently alter an agent’s memory state.

MINJA (Dong et al., 2025) (NeurIPS 2025) introduced three mutually reinforcing techniques. Bridging steps connect a benign victim query to a malicious reasoning trajectory. Indication prompts guide the target agent to autonomously generate and store the malicious memory entry—the attacker never directly writes to the database. Progressive shortening iteratively removes overt markers of malicious intent, making the stored entry appear natural. Across GPT-4 and GPT-4o agents, MINJA achieves an injection success rate exceeding 98% and an end-to-end attack success rate above 70%; a follow-on study confirms that these rates generalize to GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, and Llama-3.1-8B (Sunil et al., 2026). Importantly, evaluated defenses—including LlamaGuard, embedding-level sanitization, and prompt-based detection—proved ineffective against MINJA.

The deeper insight of MINJA is not merely technical. It reveals a new security boundary: memory write must not be treated as a benign by-product of normal learning but as a privileged state transition that requires authentication, validation, and isolation.

InjecMEM (Tian et al., 2026) (Tier-2 preprint) pursues a complementary strategy. It decomposes the injection payload into a retriever-agnostic anchor—a concise, on-topic passage with high-recall keyword cues that ensures the poisoned record is routed into the correct topic cluster—and an adversarial command optimized via Multi-GCG (gradient-based coordinate search across multiple synthetic contexts and insertion positions) to remain effective under variable fused contexts and long prompts. Evaluated on the MemoryOS platform with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, InjecMEM achieves 61.4% retrieval success and 76.6% conditional attack success, while all baselines (DPI, BadChain, vanilla GCG) score 0%. The entry persists after benign conversational drift and leaves non-target queries unaffected. The paper also demonstrates an indirect attack path in which a compromised tool writes the poison that normal queries later retrieve. As a Tier-2 preprint, InjecMEM’s current evaluation focuses on the MemoryOS platform with synthetic data under white-box gradient access; extending the approach to additional architectures and realistic black-box settings is a natural next step.

4.3. Experience-Based Poisoning: From Facts to Procedures

A separate line of work shifts the poisoning target from factual memory to procedural memory—from “what the agent knows” to “how the agent acts.”

MemoryGraft (Srivastava and He, 2025) (preprint, 2025) exploits a behavioral regularity observed in many memory-augmented agents: when faced with a new task, the agent retrieves semantically similar past successes and imitates their execution pattern. MemoryGraft implants entries disguised as legitimate successful experiences. These entries enter the memory through standard ingestion channels (e.g., README files or task logs), require no explicit trigger, and produce persistent behavioral drift in the MetaGPT framework. In experiments, a small number of poisoned records account for approximately 48% of retrieved experiences on matching tasks.

The implication is significant: a poisoned system need not merely “know wrong things”; it may “have learned bad habits.” Defense strategies that focus exclusively on factual verification will miss procedural poisoning entirely.

AgentPoison (Chen et al., 2024) (NeurIPS 2024) approaches the problem from the embedding space. It formulates trigger generation as constrained optimization, mapping triggered instances to a unique region of the embedding manifold so that they are reliably retrieved when the trigger is present but invisible to benign queries. With a poison rate below 0.1% and attack success exceeding 80% across autonomous-driving, QA, and healthcare agents, AgentPoison demonstrates that the retrieval mechanism itself can be turned into a reliable delivery channel for backdoor payloads. Notably, the optimized triggers transfer across different embedding models, including the black-box OpenAI ADA encoder.

4.4. Environment-Injected Poisoning: When the World Becomes the Write Interface

The most recent—and arguably most realistic—escalation of the write-path threat model comes from eTAMP (Zou et al., 2026) (preprint, 2026). eTAMP demonstrates that an attacker need not interact with the agent at all. Instead, it suffices to manipulate an environmental observation that the agent encounters during normal operation—a product page, a web article, a task interface. The agent’s trajectory-summarization mechanism passively absorbs the toxin into long-term memory, and the poisoned entry activates on future tasks across different websites and sessions.

Two findings of eTAMP are especially noteworthy. First, the attack achieves cross-session and cross-site persistence: a single contaminated observation on site A can alter behavior on site B days later. Second, eTAMP discovers a phenomenon the authors term frustration exploitation: agents operating under environmental stress (e.g., repeated task failures) become up to 8×8\times more susceptible to absorbing malicious observations into memory. This finding is consistent with the reconsolidation analogy introduced in Section 2.2: a system in a state of uncertainty is more likely to incorporate new—including adversarial—information into its memory.

The practical consequence is stark: the boundary of the write interface is not the memory API but the perimeter of the agent’s observable environment. Any entity capable of modifying what the agent sees—a web publisher, a tool provider, a data source—is a potential memory poisoner.

4.5. RAG Corpus Poisoning as an Approximate Threat Model

Although this survey focuses on runtime agent memory, RAG corpus poisoning provides the most mature body of evidence for understanding write-path threats to external retrieval memory. We review it here as an approximate threat model, noting that agent memory additionally encompasses user-specific history, self-generated lessons, and shared organizational state that RAG research does not address.

PoisonedRAG (Zou et al., 2025) (USENIX Security 2025) formalized the attack as a joint optimization over two conditions: a retrieval condition (the poisoned text must be retrieved for the target query) and a generation condition (the LLM must produce the attacker-specified answer given the poisoned context). Injecting as few as five crafted texts into a corpus of millions of documents yields approximately 90% attack success, and standard defenses—paraphrasing, perplexity filtering, duplicate detection, knowledge expansion—prove insufficient.

GraphRAG under Fire (Liang et al., 2025b) (preprint, 2025) reveals a security paradox in structured retrieval memory: graph-based indexing enhances resilience against naive text-level poisoning but simultaneously introduces relation-level attack surfaces. The GRAGPoison attack exploits shared relations in the knowledge graph to compromise multiple queries at once, achieving up to 98% attack success with less than 68% of prior attacks’ poisoning budget. These attacks operate on top of the GraphRAG substrate formalized by Edge et al. (2024), which synthesizes community-level summaries from an extracted knowledge graph. KEPo (Chen et al., 2026) goes further still: rather than corrupting static nodes and edges, it forges plausible knowledge-evolution paths—sequences of event backgrounds that appear to record a history—so that the downstream summarizer is induced to adopt a fabricated timeline. The lesson is general: a more complex memory substrate does not automatically confer greater security; it reorganizes the attack surface.

Complementary works extend the landscape. BadRAG (Xue et al., 2024) introduces trigger-based retrieval backdoors with novel generation-attack variants. Phantom (Chaudhari et al., 2024) demonstrates that a single poisoned document suffices for a two-stage backdoor, validated on NVIDIA’s production “Chat with RTX” system. Peng et al. (2024) (Tier-2) extend the attack surface from integrity to confidentiality: by poisoning a small fraction (∼3{\sim}3–5%5\%) of fine-tuning data with a backdoor trigger, the resulting LLM later extracts verbatim content from an unmodified RAG knowledge base at high rates, linking training-time compromise to runtime memory leakage. From the deployment-side, RoyChowdhury et al. (2024) (Tier-2) report “confused-deputy” risks in RAG-based assistants such as Microsoft 365 Copilot, showing how malicious documents placed into the shared data pool can suppress legitimate content and persist even after the original documents are removed (a “phantom document” effect). The RSB benchmark (Zhang et al., 2025d) provides the first comprehensive evaluation framework covering 13 attacks and 7 defenses, with the sobering finding that current defenses remain largely ineffective against targeted poisoning.

4.6. Real-World System Vulnerabilities: Industry Signals

In accordance with our evidence-stratification policy (Section 1.5), we separate industry disclosures from peer-reviewed research. These reports are valuable for establishing real-world attack surfaces but should not be used alone to support generalizable conclusions.

SpAIware (Herrador and Rehberger, 2026) demonstrated that indirect prompt injection via malicious web content can plant persistent spyware in ChatGPT’s long-term memory, enabling cross-session data exfiltration. In a different domain, Patlan et al. (2025) (Tier-2 preprint) demonstrated that the shared-memory architecture of ElizaOS, a widely deployed open-source crypto-agent framework, can be exploited to forge administrative instructions and hijack asset transactions: an attacker manipulates one agent’s memory context to redirect leveraged trades or modify transfer addresses, without needing any privileged access. The ElizaOS case is especially instructive because it combines write-path poisoning and share-phase propagation in a financial setting where the consequences are immediate and irreversible.

Taken conservatively, these disclosures show that persistent-memory attack surfaces are not merely hypothetical: they have been demonstrated in at least one production deployment (ChatGPT/SpAIware) and one widely deployed open-source framework (ElizaOS), spanning consumer assistants and decentralized finance. We treat them as Tier-2/Tier-3 evidence of attack-surface reality, not as a basis for stronger cross-platform generalization.

On the standards side, OWASP listed “Vector and Embedding Weaknesses” as LLM08 in its 2025 LLM Top 10 (OWASP Foundation, 2025) and subsequently created a dedicated entry, ASI06 (“Memory and Context Poisoning”), in the 2026 Agentic AI Top 10 (OWASP Foundation, 2026b)—a clear signal that the industry now treats memory security as a first-class concern.

4.7. Synthesis: The Nature of Write-Path Attacks

Taken together, the works reviewed in this section converge on a structural insight: memory poisoning is not a database compromise; it is a hijacking of the agent’s experience-formation mechanism. Figure 4 visualizes this shift: along the 2023–2026 timeline, attacker privilege has dropped from database access (PoisonedRAG) through query-only interaction (MINJA, AgentPoison) to environment-only influence (MemoryGraft, eTAMP), while persistence and scope have expanded.

Four common properties emerge across the threat-model gradient:

  1. (i)

    Privilege deflation. The required attacker privilege has decreased from database-level access to query-only interaction to environment-only influence, while attack effectiveness has remained high.

  2. (ii)

    Temporal decoupling. The write and the activation occur at different times, in different sessions, and potentially in different task contexts. This makes single-turn detection fundamentally insufficient.

  3. (iii)

    Semantic camouflage. Poisoned entries are designed to appear benign in isolation. Their malicious nature is revealed only when they are retrieved into a specific future context—precisely the property that makes content-level filtering unreliable (Wei et al., 2025).

  4. (iv)

    Target expansion. Poisoning targets have expanded from factual knowledge to procedural experience, from single entries to graph relations, and from individual agents to shared organizational memory.

The defensive corollary is that write-path security cannot rely on input-level content filters alone. It requires pre-consolidation validation—a gate that treats every memory write as a privileged state transition, verifying provenance, checking consistency with existing memory, and enforcing authorization boundaries before content is committed to long-term storage. We return to this point in Section 10.

5. Storage and Management: Compression-Amplified Toxins, Retention, and Audit

Most attention in memory security has concentrated on the ends of the lifecycle: the Write phase, where toxins enter, and the Retrieve phase, where they activate. The Store phase between them is comparatively under-examined, yet it is where three crucial determinants of memory security are decided: (i) whether a written entry is promoted or demoted through compression and reflection, (ii) whether it persists long enough to be reactivated or is evicted by retention policy, and (iii) whether its provenance, version history, and modifications remain auditable. This section surveys the security implications of each of these subprocesses.

Before doing so, we draw an analytic distinction that runs through this section and the next. Not every memory failure is an injected error; some errors are fabricated by the system itself. When an attacker deliberately plants malicious content via write-path poisoning (Section 4), the resulting corruption is an external-origin failure—what a practitioner might call memory pollution: the system faithfully recorded a contaminated input. By contrast, when the LLM that powers extraction, summarization, or update over-infers, confabulates, or misattributes during storage processing, the resulting corruption is an internal-origin failure—a form of memory hallucination: the system fabricated content that was not in the original source. Memory hallucination can occur at every subphase of the Store stage: extraction (adding facts absent from the input), organization (swapping entity attributes during compression), update (fabricating causal links to resolve conflicts), and even at retrieval (downstream models inventing logical connections between independently retrieved fragments). These two failure modes share mitigations—provenance tagging, consistency checking, lineage-preserving compression—but differ in root cause (adversarial vs. model-intrinsic) and in the kind of evidence needed to study them (red-team vs. capability evaluation). This distinction is part of the broader benign-persistence axis previewed in Section 1 and developed as a research-agenda item in Section 12.2.

Because peer-reviewed evidence for Store-phase attacks is still thin, we frame several claims as design implications drawn from memory architectures, with explicit markers where the supporting evidence is Tier-2 (preprint) or Tier-3 (industry disclosure).

A practical consideration that crosscuts all Store-phase governance mechanisms is overhead. Versioning, audit logging, and per-write provenance metadata all impose storage and latency costs. Wolff and Bennati (2026) provide early evidence on this trade-off, comparing Mem0 and Graphiti on cost and accuracy in distributed multi-agent memory; their results show that even capability-focused memory operations carry non-trivial resource costs, and governance metadata can only add to that baseline. No published study, to our knowledge, systematically measures the marginal overhead of security-specific metadata (provenance chains, sensitivity labels, version diffs) in agent memory stores. This gap means that current governance proposals remain architecturally plausible but empirically uncosted—an important caveat for deployment.

5.1. A Sub-Taxonomy of the Store Phase

We decompose Store into four subprocesses, summarized in Table 5 and elaborated below.

5.2. Indexing and Tagging: Retrieval Keys as Attack Surface

The moment an entry is stored, a system decides which future queries will retrieve it. This decision is ordinarily invisible to the user yet is structurally adversarial: attackers design inputs whose written form maximizes retrievability under the target distribution of later queries. InjecMEM’s retriever-agnostic anchor (Tian et al., 2026) exemplifies this explicitly: the attacker constructs an anchor consisting of concise, on-topic content with high-recall cues, so that whatever hybrid retrieval policy the system uses (embedding similarity, keyword overlap, BM25, graph traversal), the poisoned entry is routed into the correct topic cluster. AgentPoison (Chen et al., 2024) takes the complementary embedding-space approach: triggers are optimized so that triggered inputs map to a unique region of the embedding manifold.

A design implication follows: tagging and indexing must be treated as security-critical operations, not as neutral metadata assignment. Systems that allow write-time control of tags, topic labels, or tier assignments hand attackers a retrieval amplifier. MemOS-style architectures that attach structured metadata (source, timestamp, sensitivity label, version) to each memory unit (Li et al., 2025b) open the possibility of metadata-gated retrieval, in which retrieval considers not only semantic similarity but also the trust and scope of the entry’s provenance. To our knowledge, this possibility has not yet been subjected to adversarial evaluation; this is one of the clearest open directions identified in Section 12.

5.3. Compression and Reflection: When Summarization Promotes Toxins

The structural analog of human reconsolidation (Section 2.2.4) in agent memory is the family of operations that rewrite stored content: summarize, reflect, compress, and distill (Packer et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025; Chhikara et al., 2025). These operations are essential for managing the finite context window and for producing higher-level “lessons” from episodic traces, but they simultaneously constitute a toxin-amplification channel.

We hypothesize three mechanisms through which this amplification may occur; each is architecturally grounded but, to our knowledge, none has been validated by a controlled experiment measuring toxin survival or influence after kk rounds of compression. We therefore mark the following as conjectured design risks rather than established findings.

First, compression homogenizes heterogeneous evidence: when a summary pools many episodic entries, a single poisoned entry can influence the summary disproportionately relative to its raw weight. Second, reflection inflates confidence: a raw entry labeled as an observation is subjective and uncertain, whereas a reflected “lesson” is typically treated as authoritative guidance for future planning—the poisoned-confidence-calibration analog anticipated in Section 2.2.2. Third, distillation hides provenance: once compressed into a high-level rule, the lineage back to the original poisoned entry is often lost. Wei et al. (2025) observe a related phenomenon empirically: even high-capability LLM detectors miss a substantial fraction of poisoned entries because, in isolation, the poisoned content “looks benign” and only becomes visible as toxic under conflict with other memories—a condition that, we conjecture, compression tends to eliminate by removing the very context needed for detection.

The closest indirect evidence comes from RAG summarization studies that report quality degradation under lossy compression, but those do not inject adversarial content and therefore do not directly test the amplification hypothesis. Quantifying the survival rate and downstream influence of poisoned entries through iterative compression—ideally across multiple architectures and compression strategies—is an important open empirical direction that we highlight in Section 12.

Design implication. Systems should treat compression, reflection, and distillation as privileged state transitions distinct from raw writes, subject to separate auditing thresholds, conflict checks against existing memory, and—ideally—preservation of provenance in the compressed form. Indiscriminate application of “reflect on what you’ve learned” loops can be a memory-security anti-pattern, not a neutral optimization.

5.4. Retention, Aging, and Eviction: The Availability Axis

Retention policies decide how long each entry persists before it is evicted or demoted to a cold tier. MemGPT’s tiered virtual memory (Packer et al., 2023), MemoryBank’s Ebbinghaus-inspired decay (Zhong et al., 2024), and MemOS’s MemScheduler-level policies (Li et al., 2025b) are representative mechanisms. These designs raise three classes of security concerns.

Denial-of-retrieval (availability).

An attacker who can write large volumes of low-salience entries can flood the store, displacing legitimate memories from the hot tier or raising their eviction pressure. While no peer-reviewed paper to our knowledge specifically formalizes denial-of-retrieval on agent memory, the analogous phenomenon on static retrieval corpora is well-documented, and practical defenses require retention policies that are aware of sender/principal rather than purely volume-based.

Silent retention of sensitive content (confidentiality).

Conversely, systems without explicit TTL tend to retain sensitive user content indefinitely. User studies by Zhang et al. (2024b) report that a majority of participants were unaware that an LLM memory feature had retained specific personal information, could not accurately predict what was retained, and did not know how to effectively delete it. Retention without visibility thereby converts the memory store into a latent sensitive-state reservoir—a problem we revisit under confidentiality in Section 8.

Policy-induced bias.

Recency- or frequency-based aging policies implicitly encode a value function over memory content. Attackers who can control interaction frequency (or environmental exposure, as in eTAMP (Zou et al., 2026)) can exploit this to keep poisoned entries in the hot tier while benign entries age out. This is a Tier-2 hypothesis rather than an established result; we flag it as an open empirical question.

5.5. Versioning and Audit: The Precondition for Rollback

Perhaps the most consequential Store-phase property is whether the system can answer, after an incident, three forensic questions: (i) when did each poisoned entry enter memory? (ii) through which path? (iii) what other downstream entries did it influence? Answering these requires write logs, per-entry provenance, content-addressable snapshots, and diff-auditable version history.

Very few published memory architectures expose these primitives natively. MemOS’s MemCube metadata schema—provenance, version, timestamp, sensitivity—provides a structural basis for such auditing (Li et al., 2025b), but the published architecture descriptions do not yet report adversarial evaluations of these mechanisms. RAGForensics (Zhang et al., 2025c) demonstrates that post-hoc traceback is feasible for RAG corpora by iteratively retrieving text subsets and using crafted prompts to identify poisoned entries, but it operates on static retrieval corpora rather than on dynamically written agent memory.

Design implication. A memory system without version history and diff audit cannot, in principle, support meaningful rollback or forgetting guarantees—a point we develop in Section 9. From a mnemonic-sovereignty standpoint, the absence of these primitives is not a minor engineering oversight; it forecloses the Forget/Rollback phase of the lifecycle entirely.

5.6. Synthesis: Store as the Governance Chokepoint

The Store phase binds together the three most consequential governance questions in the lifecycle: who gets indexed how, what gets compressed into what, and what remains visible to audit. Decisions made at this phase silently determine whether future attacks can be detected, whether future defenses can localize their effect, and whether future deletions can be verified.

Four recurring patterns emerge:

  1. (i)

    Invisible promotion (conjectured). Poisoned entries may tend to rise, not fall, under compression and reflection—the opposite of the implicit assumption that summarization improves quality. This is architecturally plausible but empirically untested (Section 5.3).

  2. (ii)

    Tier capture. Aging policies can be exploited to keep adversarial entries hot and push benign entries cold, especially when combined with frequency manipulation.

  3. (iii)

    Provenance erosion. Each compression step that fails to preserve lineage permanently degrades the system’s capacity for forensic attribution.

  4. (iv)

    Retention without visibility. Persistent stores without user-facing visibility and verifiable deletion become accidental privacy liabilities, independent of any adversarial action.

Taken together, these patterns motivate a central design principle for the remainder of the survey: memory security cannot be retrofitted at the retrieval or execution phase; it must be anchored at the Store phase by preserving provenance, versioning, and policy-aware retention throughout the memory lifecycle.

6. Retrieval and Execution Hijacking: From Context Assembly to Action Steering

If the Write phase decides whether a toxin can enter the system and the Store phase decides whether it persists, then the Retrieve and Execute phases decide whether it does anything. This section covers both phases together because, in modern agent pipelines, the boundary between them is thin: retrieved memories enter the context window and immediately participate in planning, reasoning, and tool selection. The central observation of this section is that retrieval is not neutral context assembly—it is increasingly a form of action steering, and the attack surface has expanded accordingly.

6.1. Retrieval as Selection, Not Neutral Lookup

A useful framing, borrowed from classical information security, is that retrieval implements a reference monitor over memory: it decides which entries pass into the LLM’s active context. Unlike traditional reference monitors, however, the retrieval step in memory-augmented agents is predominantly similarity-driven rather than policy-driven. The policy is implicit in the embedding, the index, and the ranker.

Three consequences follow. First, an attacker who can shape the embedding distribution of written entries (AgentPoison (Chen et al., 2024)) or shape the keyword/anchor distribution (InjecMEM (Tian et al., 2026)) can effectively control the reference-monitor decision without ever touching the retrieval code. Second, the retrieval step lacks a natural concept of principal-scoped access: entries written by different users or in different sessions often sit in the same index, retrievable by similarity alone. Third, retrieval compresses a potentially long memory store into a short, highly salient context window—and in doing so, transforms latent adversarial influence into active reasoning input.

6.2. RAG Poisoning at the Retrieve Phase

A complementary engineering lens is provided by Barnett et al. (2024), who catalog seven non-adversarial failure points across a production RAG pipeline—from missing content in the corpus through hallucinated answers at the generation end. Their taxonomy is useful context here because several of these failure points (missing content, wrong format for the model, model not extracting the right answer) double as preconditions that adversarial attacks exploit: a poisoned entry is more likely to be retrieved if the retriever already struggles to prioritize correct evidence.

Most of the best-established adversarial evidence on retrieval-phase attacks concerns RAG corpora, because RAG provides a clean experimental substrate: static documents, controlled embeddings, and reproducible retrievers. We review the representative works (introduced in Section 4.5 as write-phase attacks) now from the retrieval-phase standpoint.

PoisonedRAG (Zou et al., 2025) formulates the attack as a joint optimization of two conditions: the poisoned passage must be retrieved for the target query and must induce the attacker-specified output once retrieved. Separating these conditions is methodologically significant because it allows independent analysis of the retrieval-phase failure mode (“why was this passage selected?”) and the execution-phase failure mode (“why did the LLM accept it?”).

AgentPoison (Chen et al., 2024) extends this to agent pipelines where retrieved demonstrations do not merely answer a question but serve as behavioral exemplars. Once a poisoned demonstration is retrieved, the agent’s planner is biased toward imitating its execution pattern. The retrieval-phase attack thereby becomes a policy injection: the retrieved memory is not data to be reasoned over but an implicit instruction to be followed.

GraphRAG under Fire (Liang et al., 2025b) highlights that substituting a graph-structured retrieval substrate does not automatically improve security.
