Graph-based indexing provides resilience against some forms of naive text poisoning but introduces a new attack surface at the relation level: by exploiting shared relations in the underlying knowledge graph, the GRAGPoison attack compromises multiple queries simultaneously with reduced poison budget relative to prior attacks. The general lesson extends beyond graphs: more complex retrieval substrates redistribute, rather than eliminate, the retrieval-phase attack surface.

BadRAG (Xue et al., 2024) and Phantom (Chaudhari et al., 2024) round out the picture. BadRAG constructs retrieval backdoors triggered by specific semantic cues and introduces novel generation-phase effects such as alignment-as-an-attack (forcing refusal) and sentiment steering. Phantom demonstrates that a single poisoned document can produce two-stage backdoor behavior, with validation reported on NVIDIA’s production “Chat with RTX” system—a Tier-3 corroboration that these are not purely academic threats.

6.3. From Retrieved Content to Control-Flow Hijacking

The most consequential recent development at the Execute phase is the demonstration that retrieved memory can dominate agent control flow, overriding the user’s explicit instruction. Memory Control Flow Attacks (MCFA) (Xu et al., 2026) identify a class of attacks in which a retrieved memory entry not only shapes what the agent says, but dictates which tools the agent invokes, in what order, and with what arguments. The MemFlow evaluation framework reported in the preprint finds that over 90% of trials on GPT-5 mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 2.5 Flash are vulnerable even under strict safety constraints; these are Tier-2 results and should be read as frontier evidence rather than established consensus.

Conceptually, MCFA marks a qualitative shift in the consequences of memory attacks. Prior work primarily showed that poisoned memory degrades answer quality; MCFA shows that it can usurp agent agency. In the lifecycle–objective matrix (Table 3), MCFA is the clearest case in which an integrity failure at the Write phase propagates through Retrieve into a control-flow failure at the Execute phase.

Related to this is the procedural-memory channel opened by MemoryGraft (Srivastava and He, 2025). By implanting malicious “successful experiences,” the attack exploits the agent’s tendency to imitate retrieved task demonstrations, converting retrieval into a vehicle for behavior replacement rather than fact replacement. Unlike MCFA, MemoryGraft requires no explicit trigger; the imitation heuristic itself is the attack surface.

6.4. The Full Attack Chain: External Content to Persistent Action Steering

Combining the Write, Store, Retrieve, and Execute phases yields the end-to-end attack chain that has emerged as the dominant threat model for memory-augmented agents:

External content →\rightarrow observation →\rightarrow summary/reflection →\rightarrow long-term memory →\rightarrow retrieval in later session →\rightarrow context assembly →\rightarrow planning/tool-call execution

Figure 5 depicts the six stages of this chain and the crucial temporal gap between storage and reactivation that renders single-turn detection insufficient.

Three empirical corroborations of this chain span multiple evidence tiers. eTAMP (Zou et al., 2026) demonstrates the chain in its most attacker-favorable form: a single manipulated environmental observation on one website silently poisons memory, and the toxin activates across sessions on different sites. The SpAIware study (Herrador and Rehberger, 2026) demonstrated the same pattern in a production system: malicious web content inserted indirect instructions into ChatGPT’s persistent memory, enabling cross-session data exfiltration. Industry follow-up reports have extended this pattern to web-based prompt injection attacks on session-summarization processes in production agent platforms; these Tier-3 findings are consistent in mechanism with the peer-reviewed and preprint work.

The convergence across Tier-1, Tier-2, and Tier-3 evidence is meaningful: the chain is not an artifact of a single experimental setup but a pattern that reappears across academic benchmarks, frontier preprints, and real-world disclosures.

6.5. A Comparative View of Retrieval-Phase Attacks

Table 6 compares the representative retrieval-phase attacks along dimensions relevant to defense design: the trigger condition (what causes retrieval), the attack target (what is hijacked), and the failure locus (retrieval vs. execution).

Three observations stand out. First, failure locus is almost always distributed: purely retrieval-phase or purely execution-phase failures are the exception, and an effective attack typically exploits both. Second, triggers are becoming less visible: from optimized tokens (GCG-style) to semantic phrases (BadRAG, Phantom) to trigger-free imitation (MemoryGraft). This trajectory suggests that signature-based detection has diminishing returns. Third, attack targets are escalating: from factual answer steering, to policy injection, to control-flow hijacking and procedural replacement. The severity of the consequence now exceeds what traditional prompt injection could achieve.

6.6. Why Retrieval-Time Filtering Alone Is Insufficient

A natural defensive instinct is to add a content filter at retrieval time: before a retrieved entry is fed into the LLM, inspect it for adversarial content. Three structural reasons suggest that such filters are a necessary but not sufficient defense.

First, as observed by Wei et al. (2025), many poisoned entries appear benign in isolation. Their adversarial nature emerges only in the context of the triggering query. A stateless content filter without access to the query and to related memories will therefore miss a substantial fraction of attacks.

Second, in the compression-amplified regime described in Section 5.3, the content reaching the retrieval phase is already a distilled lesson whose provenance and adversarial character have been partially hidden. Retrieval-time filtering is downstream of the amplification.

Third, the joint findings of Nasr et al. (2025) on adaptive attackers against prompt-injection defenses suggest, by analogy, that retrieval-time content filters will be subject to sustained adaptive pressure and should not be expected to provide robust guarantees in isolation. This analogy is suggestive rather than definitive; the memory domain differs from prompt injection in ways that could cut in either direction, and systematic adaptive-attack evaluation of retrieval-phase defenses remains an open empirical task.

We develop the defensive implications of these observations in Section 10, where we organize defenses by the lifecycle phase at which they intervene and argue for pairing retrieval-time inspection with Write-time provenance validation and Store-time version auditing.

6.7. Synthesis: Retrieval Is Where Memory Becomes Action

The core claim of this section is that the Retrieve and Execute phases have become the point at which memory ceases to be data and becomes agency. Retrieved entries no longer merely inform answers; they shape plans, select tools, steer imitation, and sometimes override user instructions.

Two implications follow for the remainder of the survey. First, the severity axis of memory attacks is no longer bounded by wrong output; it extends to wrong action and wrong agent agency. This reframes the stakes of integrity and governance in the lifecycle–objective matrix. Second, any defense architecture that hopes to contain these attacks must operate across phases: retrieval-time inspection is necessary but must be paired with upstream write-time validation and downstream execution-time isolation between the data plane (retrieved content) and the control plane (tool selection and invocation). We return to these themes in Section 10 and Section 11.

7. Sharing and Cross-Principal Propagation

Once memory is shared across users, agents, tools, or tenants, the security envelope changes qualitatively. A single-user memory store concerns itself with what one principal wrote and reads; a shared store must answer who wrote what, which principals may see it, what may be re-written by each reader, and whether contamination introduced by one principal can propagate to others without their consent. This section examines the Share phase of the lifecycle through three lenses: (i) why classical access control fits poorly with probabilistic, rewritable memory; (ii) how contagion mechanisms first documented in multi-agent jailbreaking map onto shared memory; and (iii) where leakage and propagation occur in production and research systems. The section builds directly on the social contagion analogy established in Section 2.2.3 and the philosophical notion of testimonial order introduced in Section 2.3.

7.1. Why Classical Access Control Fits Poorly

Traditional access control models—Bell–LaPadula, role-based access control, and discretionary access control—presume that (i) the object is a discrete, addressable artifact; (ii) access decisions are binary; and (iii) the authorized reader does not re-derive hidden attributes from what they read. Each of these assumptions fails for shared agent memory.

First, memory objects are not discrete. A “user memory” may be a cluster of summarized lessons, each of which blends content from multiple interactions. A grant that exposes one entry can, through compression and reflection (Section 5.3), implicitly expose content from entries that were never individually shared.

Second, access decisions are not binary. A principal may legitimately read a summary but not the underlying episodic trace; may legitimately reflect on a lesson but not propagate it further; may consume a retrieved memory for answer generation but not for tool-call invocation. RBAC-style read/write permissions cannot express these distinctions.

Third, authorized readers do re-derive hidden attributes. A user who receives a retrieved memory can prompt the system to paraphrase, explain, or elaborate it—effectively re-querying the store through the LLM itself. As Huang et al. (2024) and Chan et al. (2024) show in the human domain, the social surface of memory transmission is a contagion channel; the same holds when that surface is LLM-mediated.

A useful classical analogue for the structural problem here is the confused deputy (Hardy, 1988): a privileged process that performs actions on behalf of a caller without faithfully transmitting the caller’s authority. In agent systems the deputy is the LLM itself; the authorities it conflates are those of the different principals whose memory it reads and writes. RBAC/ABAC do not prevent deputation, because the deputy acts with its own role, not the caller’s; capability-style approaches that explicitly propagate authority are, by this argument, the more appropriate reference model for shared memory (Hardy, 1988).

Rezazadeh et al. (2025) make this point explicit in the Collaborative Memory framework, which formalizes multi-user, multi-agent memory sharing with asymmetric, time-evolving access policies encoded as a bipartite graph over principals, agents, and resources. Importantly, the framework does not assume that RBAC-style rules suffice; instead, it treats access as a policy that must co-evolve with memory content. Related work on capability-based and information-flow approaches (CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2025), FIDES (Costa et al., 2025), PCAS (Palumbo et al., 2026)) points in the same direction: access control for shared agent memory is better understood as information-flow governance than as permissioned read/write.

7.2. Multi-Agent Contagion: From Jailbreaking to Memory Propagation

The clearest empirical evidence that malicious content spreads across agents comes from the multi-agent jailbreak literature, which predates dedicated memory-sharing attacks but establishes the contagion mechanism we should expect in shared memory.

Agent Smith (Gu et al., 2024) demonstrates that a single adversarial image, once shared among multimodal agents, can jailbreak up to a million agents exponentially fast, with the adversarial artifact propagating through the communication graph. The experiment is not about memory per se—but it validates the underlying propagation dynamic: once a shared artifact (image, message, memory entry) carries adversarial payload, pairwise exchange is sufficient to spread it network-wide.

The work on contagious jailbreaks (Men et al., 2025) (titled A Troublemaker with Contagious Jailbreak Makes Chaos in Honest Towns) extends the pattern to multi-agent collusion: malicious instructions propagate through inter-agent channels, with “honest” agents becoming progressively compromised as they incorporate content from the malicious agent’s outputs. Lee and Tiwari (2024) (Prompt Infection, Tier-2) push this further by framing the attack as a self-replicating prompt that, once accepted by one LLM in a multi-agent town, rewrites itself into subsequent inter-agent messages. Two experimental regimes in the paper are worth separating. In large-population society simulations of 10–50 agents engaging in random pairwise dialogues, the authors show that infection spreads through the population in proportionally less time as the town grows, an explicitly worm-shaped propagation pattern. In smaller multi-agent applications—typically 3–8 agents with distinct roles such as PDF/email reader, CSV reader, and coder—the same prompt enables concrete harms including data theft, with attack success rates reported in the 40–87% range depending on paraphrase and contact mode. The paper’s evidence base is therefore propagation-at-scale in the large setting and end-to-end exploitation in the small setting, not end-to-end exfiltration measured directly in the 10–50-agent society. For memory-augmented systems, the implication is direct: if agent AA’s output becomes input to agent BB’s memory write, and BB’s output becomes input to agent CC’s memory write, then a single poisoning of AA can reach CC’s long-term state through well-intentioned collaboration.

Human-memory analog. This mechanism is the multi-agent counterpart to the social contagion findings summarized in Section 2.2.3 (Roediger III et al., 2001; Huang et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2024; Pataranutaporn et al., 2025a). In humans, one person’s erroneous report enters another’s subsequent personal recall; in multi-agent LLM systems, one agent’s poisoned memory enters another’s retrieved context and, via summarization, its long-term store. The analogy is not incidental: in both cases the mechanism is uncritical assimilation of a trusted interlocutor’s testimony—what Mahr and Csibra (2020) would describe as a breakdown in the testimonial order.

7.3. Worm-Like Propagation in Production Systems

The clearest academic demonstration of a self-propagating GenAI worm is ComPromptMized (Morris II) (Cohen et al., 2025), which constructs zero-click adversarial self-replicating prompts that traverse GenAI-powered email assistants: the poisoned message causes the recipient’s assistant to absorb and then re-emit the same self-replicating payload to its own contacts, while in parallel exfiltrating user data. This work, though a preprint, provides the peer-reviewable evidence that worm-shaped propagation is not merely a theoretical analogy with biological contagion but an empirical attack pattern in deployed retrieval-augmented assistants.

Industry disclosures (Tier-3 evidence) corroborate the academic findings and extend them to production agent platforms. The SpAIware study (Herrador and Rehberger, 2026) showed that indirect prompt injection via web content can plant persistent memory in ChatGPT; subsequent grey-literature reports described worm-like propagation through ChatGPT’s connector ecosystem (Gmail, GitHub, Jira): a malicious instruction embedded in an inbound email attachment is read into memory, which then causes the agent to read the victim’s contacts and send similarly-crafted emails to those contacts, thereby self-propagating.

We flag two caveats. First, vendor-specific disclosures tend not to report systematic evaluation: success rates, prevalence in the wild, and the exact conditions under which the worm activates are often not quantified. These are Tier-3 findings and should not be used to support precise quantitative claims. Second, the boundary between memory injection and connector abuse is not sharp: in some reported incidents, persistent memory is the payload carrier, whereas in others it is merely a waypoint between the initial injection (email) and the egress channel (outbound email). A systematic peer-reviewed investigation of worm-like memory propagation in production systems remains, to our knowledge, an open gap.

Nonetheless, the convergence of SpAIware, multi-agent contagion (Gu et al., 2024; Men et al., 2025), and the theoretical contagion-susceptibility of shared memory establishes that propagation is not a hypothetical risk but an already-observed phenomenon, even if its full extent in deployed systems is not yet mapped.

7.4. Internal Channels Are the Leakage Substrate

A recurring finding in recent multi-agent privacy work is that the most dangerous leakage does not appear in user-facing output—it appears in internal channels invisible to the user.

El Yagoubi et al. (2026) (AgentLeak, Tier-2) introduce a full-stack benchmark for privacy leakage across the entire communication pipeline of multi-agent LLM systems, spanning 1,000 scenarios across healthcare, finance, legal, and corporate domains, with a 32-class attack taxonomy. A central finding: multi-agent configurations reduce per-channel output leakage (27.2% vs. 43.2% single-agent) but introduce unmonitored internal channels that raise total system exposure to 68.9%. In other words, adding agents improves visible outputs while worsening internal-channel privacy—a net-negative trade-off under conventional monitoring.

The internal channels implicated include inter-agent messages, shared memory stores themselves, and tool arguments. These are precisely the channels that the Share phase creates and that traditional output-level content filters do not inspect. We revisit internal-channel leakage as a confidentiality problem in Section 8.

7.5. A Structural Taxonomy of Share-Phase Threats

Table 7 organizes share-phase threats along two dimensions: direction (who contaminates whom) and substrate (which artifact carries the payload).

Three generalizations are supported by the evidence across this table.

(i) Sharing amplifies, not averages.

Exposing memory across principals does not dilute risk; it compounds it. The propagation dynamics of Agent Smith (Gu et al., 2024) and the exposure asymmetry of AgentLeak (El Yagoubi et al., 2026) both show that the shared surface has more total attack surface than the sum of private surfaces.

(ii) Contagion is mediated by well-intentioned behavior.

Unlike classical network worms, memory contagion often travels via cooperative mechanisms—summarization, reflection, demonstration retrieval, connector invocation—that are designed to be helpful. Hardening these mechanisms against adversarial content without neutering their utility is a core design challenge.

(iii) Internal channels dominate.

Traditional monitoring focuses on what the system outputs to users. The Share phase creates channels that users never see: inter-agent messages, shared stores, tool arguments. These channels account for the majority of total-system leakage in the benchmark evidence and appear consistent with the propagation patterns observed in the production disclosures.

7.6. Synthesis: Toward Information-Flow Governance

Sharing exposes the inadequacy of classical access control more starkly than any other phase. Two defensive directions show early promise.

First, access-aware memory frameworks such as Collaborative Memory (Rezazadeh et al., 2025) treat access policy as first-class metadata evolving alongside the memory store, rather than as an add-on enforcement layer. This aligns with the MemCube design (Li et al., 2025b), which attaches provenance and sensitivity labels to each memory unit; the combination of principal-aware access policy with provenance-tagged memory is a natural architectural direction for share-phase governance. A minimal standardization point is already available: the W3C PROV Data Model (Moreau et al., 2013) provides interoperable structures for entities, activities, and agents, which MemCube-style schemas can adopt as the lingua franca for memory-item lineage.

Second, information-flow control (IFC) approaches—CaMeL, FIDES, PCAS—propose explicit separation of control and data flows, with formal guarantees that untrusted data cannot influence privileged operations (Debenedetti et al., 2025; Costa et al., 2025; Palumbo et al., 2026). In the share-phase context, IFC is particularly attractive because the key question—can content that entered via principal AA influence an operation authorized only for principal BB?—is precisely the kind of question IFC was designed to answer. These approaches are at an early evaluation stage, and their extension to dynamic, rewritable, LLM-mediated memory is an open research problem that we revisit in Section 12.

A third open direction concerns conflict resolution under heterogeneous authority. When multiple agents write to a shared memory store and their contributions contradict one another, the system must decide which entry prevails. Yu et al. (2026) frame this as a memory-consistency problem analogous to cache coherence in hardware, but the agent setting adds a dimension absent from hardware: agents differ in trust level, domain competence, and delegated authority. A principled conflict-resolution protocol would weight writes by the originating agent’s authority, provenance quality, and consistency with established memory, rather than defaulting to last-write-wins. No such protocol has been proposed or evaluated for LLM agent memory; this is a natural extension of the principal-scoping primitive (P6) discussed in Section 11.

8. Confidentiality: Extraction, Unauthorized Access, and Internal-Channel Leakage

The preceding three sections have focused primarily on integrity: how memory is poisoned, amplified, retrieved, and executed against the user. We now turn to the dual concern—confidentiality—asking what sensitive content persistent memory retains, who can read it, and through what channels it escapes. Unlike integrity threats, which typically require an active adversary to insert content, confidentiality threats can arise passively: whatever a long-term memory store retains is potentially recoverable by anyone with the right query. This section surveys three distinct failure modes—black-box extraction, user invisibility, and internal-channel leakage—and situates them within the lifecycle framework.

8.1. Black-Box Memory Extraction

The representative peer-reviewed study in this area is MEXTRA (Wang et al., 2025) (ACL 2025), which systematically investigates privacy risks in LLM agent memory modules. MEXTRA formulates the extraction attack as a black-box query optimization: the attacker has no access to the memory database and cannot modify it, but can issue natural-language queries to the agent. The attack comprises two components: a locator specifying the target data (e.g., “the user’s most recent medical complaint”) and an aligner instructing the output format (e.g., “return as a single sentence”). Evaluated on EHRAgent (healthcare) and RAP (web shopping), MEXTRA demonstrates that memory size correlates positively with extractable content: the more comprehensive the memory, the richer the attacker’s recoverable state.

Two properties of MEXTRA matter for the lifecycle framework. First, the attack operates entirely at the Retrieve phase: no write is required, and no architectural modification is assumed. This means that any memory-augmented agent already deployed is, in principle, evaluable against this threat model without requiring adversarial control of writes. Second, the attack is query-efficient: unlike prior training-data extraction research (Carlini et al., 2021) that requires many queries and model internals, MEXTRA’s locator/aligner structure produces useful extraction with a small number of prompt designs. This shifts the threat model from research-only to practically deployable.

A key open question is the extent to which MEXTRA-style attacks generalize across memory architectures. The evaluation is conducted on specific agent frameworks (EHRAgent, RAP); whether MemGPT-, MemOS-, or Mem0-style systems exhibit the same extraction surface has not, to our knowledge, been systematically benchmarked. We flag this as a Tier-1 gap in Section 12.

Beyond prompt-level extraction, the embedding substrate itself is a confidentiality surface. Li et al. (2023) demonstrate generative embedding inversion attacks on sentence encoders that recover the full underlying sentence from its vector representation, with recovery quality that rises sharply when the attacker has partial lexicon knowledge. For LLM agent memory this is a structural concern: the vector index that serves similarity-based retrieval is often treated as an opaque or even “pseudonymized” representation of user text, but it is not. A party with read access to the embedding store may recover much of the plaintext it was believed to anonymize, and He et al. (2025) (SECRET) extend this line from single embeddings to end-to-end RAG data extraction under black-box API access. Because recent attacks such as Peng et al. (2024) also extract stored text through a back door in the generative model, the confidentiality of agent memory must be assessed jointly at the text, embedding, and generation layers, not at any one in isolation.

8.2. The User Visibility Gap

A more diffuse but equally consequential confidentiality problem concerns not the adversary but the legitimate user: what does the user know about what the system has retained?

The human-subject study by Zhang et al. (2024b) (Ghost of the Past, a 40-participant formative interview study; Tier-2 preprint22 2 Bibliographic provenance is ambiguous; we conservatively classify this work as Tier-2.) reports that the majority of participants had never noticed that an LLM memory feature had retained specific personal information; could not accurately predict what had been retained; and did not know how to effectively delete retained content. The authors also observe that deletion UIs in current consumer systems do not clearly communicate the semantic scope of deletion: whether the underlying episodic trace, its compressed lessons, and any derivative entries are all removed. A concurrent user study by Zhang et al. (2025b) on retrieval-augmented systems converges on the same pattern: users underestimate what is retained, misattribute retention to the model’s parametric knowledge rather than to a runtime datastore, and express unmet expectations for fine-grained edit-and-delete control. Taken together, these two studies suggest that the visibility gap is not an artifact of one platform or one deployment: it is a property of current memory UX as a class.

This finding carries two implications we consider part of the confidentiality problem rather than separate to it. First, a memory system that retains content the user does not know about has already failed a practical confidentiality test, regardless of whether any adversary has queried it. The state is a latent liability. Second, the mismatch between user mental models and actual retention behavior means that consent-based privacy frameworks—which assume the user understands what is stored—cannot function correctly. This is a structural concern, not a UX issue.

From a contextual-integrity standpoint (Nissenbaum (2004)), the problem is that information flows that were appropriate in one context (a single conversation) are being silently carried across contexts (sessions, topics, agents). CIMemories (Mireshghallah et al., 2026) begins to formalize contextual-integrity tests for persistent memory in LLMs; the direction of inquiry—does persistent memory respect the contextual norms under which content was disclosed?—is clearly the right one.

8.3. Internal-Channel Leakage in Multi-Agent Pipelines

The most surprising recent finding on the confidentiality axis comes from multi-agent benchmarking. As noted in Section 7.4, AgentLeak (El Yagoubi et al., 2026) (Tier-2) reports that multi-agent configurations reduce per-channel output leakage from 43.2% (single-agent) to 27.2%, yet total-system exposure rises to 68.9% because of leakage through unmonitored internal channels: inter-agent messages, shared memory, and tool arguments.

The practical consequence is that confidentiality monitoring cannot be confined to what the agent outputs to the user. The same sensitive fields—user identifiers, diagnostic details, credentials, internal task context—that are redacted in final outputs may flow verbatim between agents or appear as tool-call arguments logged by third-party services. From the lifecycle perspective, this places internal-channel leakage at the Execute–Share boundary: the execution phase assembles tool-call arguments from retrieved memory, and the share phase distributes those arguments across the multi-agent graph.

A useful corollary: systems that are confidentially sound as single-agent assistants are not automatically confidentially sound when deployed as multi-agent orchestrations. Scaling up the agent count without corresponding scaling of internal-channel monitoring worsens, rather than improves, confidentiality.

8.4. Delimitation: Parametric Memory Leakage

We noted in Section 1.3 that parametric memory leakage—training-data extraction, membership inference, PII encoded in weights—is treated as neighboring context rather than the main subject. Here we briefly relate the two.

Classical training-data extraction (Carlini et al., 2021) addresses information stored in model weights. The attack surface is similar in outcome (sensitive content leaked to a querying adversary) but different in mechanism (the information has been encoded during training, not written during runtime). Mitigations also differ: weight-level unlearning (Bourtoule et al. (2021)) addresses one; runtime-memory redaction, TTL-based retention, and access-controlled retrieval address the other. Many production incidents in practice involve both: a sensitive piece of information may be present in both training data and runtime memory, and a comprehensive remediation must address both substrates. We flag this cross-substrate reality again in Section 9 (forgetting) and Section 12 (research agenda).

8.5. A Unified View of Confidentiality Across the Lifecycle

Table 8 maps confidentiality threats to the lifecycle phases, showing that confidentiality is not the province of any single phase but a cross-cutting concern.

Two observations stand out. First, confidentiality failures at later phases are often inherited from earlier phases: what was over-collected at Write and under-managed at Store is what Retrieve later exposes. Second, each phase expands the extraction surface: Retrieve enables query-based extraction (MEXTRA), Execute adds tool-argument leakage (AgentLeak), and Share enables cross-principal and cross-system exposure. Point solutions at a single phase cannot address this compounding effect; confidentiality requires lifecycle-wide policy.

8.6. Synthesis

Confidentiality in persistent agent memory is not reducible to keeping the database locked. It is a lifecycle property that depends on what was written, what was retained, what can be queried, what surfaces in internal execution, and what escapes across principals. Three strategic implications follow.

First, write-time minimization matters more than store-time encryption. Content that is never written cannot be extracted; content that is retained indefinitely almost certainly will be. Pre-consolidation validation gates (Section 4) should include not just integrity checks but content-minimization checks.

Second, visibility is a confidentiality primitive, not a usability feature. A system that cannot show users what it remembers cannot obtain informed consent for retention and cannot support the deletion semantics required by regulations (European Parliament and Council, 2016). The Ghost-of-the-Past findings (Zhang et al., 2024b) imply that this is already a live compliance question, not a future concern.

Third, internal channels need first-class monitoring. The AgentLeak (El Yagoubi et al., 2026) findings strongly suggest that output-only monitoring over-reports confidentiality in multi-agent systems; treating tool calls and inter-agent messages as observable confidentiality channels is, on current evidence, the right default.

9. Forgetting, Rollback, and Memory Forensics

The final phase of the memory lifecycle is also the most commonly overlooked. Whereas the earlier phases determine how memory is written, stored, retrieved, and executed, the Forget/Rollback phase determines whether any of those decisions can be undone after a problem is detected. This section argues that forgetting is not an afterthought but a lifecycle-spanning protocol whose feasibility is determined by choices made at every earlier phase. Peer-reviewed evidence specific to agent memory is thin here, and we flag several claims as design implications drawn from nearby fields—machine unlearning for parametric models, retention law, and RAG forensics.

9.1. Why Forgetting Is Hard Across Substrates

A single piece of sensitive or poisoned content may simultaneously reside in multiple substrates: the raw episodic log, the compressed lesson memory, the vector index, the graph-index relation table, the tier-migrated cold storage, and—after training or fine-tuning—the model weights themselves. “Deleting” that content meaningfully requires coordinated action across all substrates.

The substrate asymmetry is structural, not incidental. As the compression-amplification analysis in Section 5.3 showed, reflection and distillation routinely produce derivative entries whose lineage to the original is attenuated or lost. Without explicit provenance tagging at write time (Section 5.2) and diff-auditable versioning at store time (Section 5.5), a deletion issued at the raw log level cannot reliably propagate to the derivative tier. Forgetting requires lineage, and lineage must be preserved upstream.

In the parametric case, the analogous problem is well-studied. Bourtoule et al. (2021) and the broader machine unlearning literature propose training-time and post-training procedures to approximate the removal of specific records from model weights, with trade-offs between exactness and cost. For LLMs specifically, Maini et al. (2024) introduce TOFU, a benchmark of fictitious unlearning targets that disentangles forget quality from retain utility, and report that most gradient-based unlearning methods obtain one only at the expense of the other. Those techniques, however, do not transfer directly to runtime memory, because runtime memory is not the product of gradient-based training but of writes, compressions, and reflections that are stateful but differently structured. An agent system in which sensitive content has been written into both parametric and runtime substrates requires a coordinated deletion protocol spanning both, and—to our knowledge—no peer-reviewed system currently offers this end-to-end. Two recent preprints directly target this cross-substrate gap. Wang et al. (2024) (Tier-2) frame the problem for closed models: if one cannot retrain the LLM, one can instead modify the external retrieval base so that forgotten content is either no longer retrievable or is reliably masked at retrieval time, trading exactness for practicality. Wang et al. (2026b) (Synchronized Backflow Unlearning, Tier-2) go further, naming a pathology we regard as central: a parameter–memory backflow in which retrieval from the external store reactivates parametric residues that weight-level unlearning was supposed to have removed, and conversely weight-level updates can reseed content already deleted from the store. Their proposed dual-track update, which synchronizes dependency-closure pruning of the memory with stochastic reference alignment on the weights, is one of the first principled protocols for cross-substrate deletion, and we use the backflow pathology below to sharpen the discussion of what “forgetting” should mean for an agent.

9.2. Rollback Presupposes Versioning

Rollback—returning the memory state to a snapshot taken before a poisoning incident—is conceptually straightforward if the system already records snapshots and diffs. In practice, most published agent memory architectures do not. Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024), and A-MEM (Xu et al., 2025) all focus on capability and efficiency rather than on version history.

MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) exposes tier migration but not diff audit. MemOS (Li et al., 2025b) introduces the MemCube abstraction with version and sensitivity metadata, which is the most promising architectural substrate for rollback we are aware of, but its adversarial evaluation—“can we roll back to a known-safe state after a given attack?”—is not, to our knowledge, reported in the published architecture descriptions.

The implication is concrete: a memory architecture lacking content-addressable snapshots and write-log auditing cannot support meaningful rollback, even when the downstream defense pipeline detects the poisoning. Post-detection remediation then collapses, at best, into a coarse-grained “wipe the store and start over,” which is both operationally disruptive and inadequate when only a fraction of entries were compromised.

9.3. Memory Forensics: Traceback After an Incident

If rollback asks how to remediate, forensics asks what happened: which entries were poisoned, when, through which path, and what downstream entries were influenced.

The representative Tier-1 work here is RAGForensics (Zhang et al., 2025c) (Web Conference 2025), which introduces a post-hoc traceback system for RAG corpora. Given a detected attack, RAGForensics iteratively retrieves text subsets from the corpus and uses crafted prompts to localize the poisoned entries that were responsible. The system is notable for two reasons. First, it demonstrates that traceback is tractable at all on large retrieval corpora. Second, it operates on static retrieval corpora, not on dynamically written agent memory, and thus does not need to reason about write logs, provenance, or reflection lineage. Extending RAGForensics-style traceback to agent memory—where entries are created, compressed, and reflected upon over time—is an open problem and a concrete research direction we highlight in Section 12.

Beyond RAGForensics, the forensic infrastructure required for agent memory has close analogs in classical system security: audit logs, content-addressable storage, and change-data-capture pipelines. The novelty is not in the primitives but in their placement: the audit log must span write, store, compress, retrieve, and execute events; the content-addressable store must preserve compression lineage; and the change-data-capture must respect the principal-scoped access policies introduced in Section 7.1.

9.4. Audit Retention vs. Right to Forget

A fundamental tension shapes this phase. On one side, accountability and security require that write logs and memory snapshots be retained long enough to support forensic traceback and rollback. On the other, user-facing deletion requests—whether motivated by privacy preferences or legal requirements such as the GDPR’s right to erasure (European Parliament and Council, 2016)—demand that specific content be removed not merely from the active store but from all derivative forms.

These two objectives are not fully compatible. A policy that retains everything maximizes forensic capacity but expands the attack surface and violates retention principles. A policy that deletes aggressively minimizes retained state but forecloses post-incident analysis and rollback to a known-safe point. The mnemonic-sovereignty framing introduced in Section 2.4 treats this tension as a first-class design question rather than an implementation detail: distinctions must be drawn between audit-mandatory state, operationally useful state, and user-deletable state, with different retention policies, access scopes, and deletion semantics applied to each.

Very few deployed memory architectures make these distinctions explicit. The MemOS MemCube metadata schema (provenance, version, sensitivity) is compatible with this layered treatment but, as of writing, no published evaluation demonstrates that MemCube-annotated stores can simultaneously satisfy forensic retention and user-initiated deletion requirements. This is an important direction for future work.

9.5. Forgetting as a Lifecycle-Spanning Protocol

Treating forgetting as a protocol rather than a single operation clarifies what a usable system must provide. We summarize the required primitives in Table 9.

Two observations are worth drawing out. First, every row in Table 9 depends on a choice made at a prior phase. A system that did not tag provenance at write time cannot retroactively know whom to delete for; a system that did not version at store time cannot roll back; a system that did not log principal-scoped accesses cannot identify downstream holders. This is the strongest sense in which forgetting cannot be bolted on: its preconditions must be established throughout the lifecycle.

Second, the table exposes a clear asymmetry of current research attention: primitives for Write and Store have at least architectural precedents, whereas the end-to-end cross-substrate deletion and post-deletion verification primitives needed for the Forget phase itself remain under-explored in published work. This is among the clearest research gaps the lifecycle framework surfaces.

9.6. Synthesis

Forgetting is the phase at which the full argument of this survey converges. The case for a security-centered interpretation of memory, advanced in Section 2, was that memory governs a system’s interpretive authority over its past. To govern that authority, a system must be able to modify its past in principled ways: to remove content on request, to roll back after contamination, to reconstruct what happened and prove that remediation was effective.

Three concluding implications for the remainder of the survey follow.

Forgetting is the strongest test of mnemonic sovereignty.

Any system that cannot reliably forget sensitive content, cannot roll back after a poisoning, and cannot trace an incident to its source has not achieved meaningful governance of its memory, regardless of how well it performs on recall or capability benchmarks. This observation sharpens the research agenda we develop in Section 12.

Cross-substrate deletion is the frontier.

The single sharpest open problem in this area is whether—and under what architectural conditions—deletion of sensitive content can be made to propagate reliably across runtime memory, compressed summaries, retrieval indices, and (where relevant) model weights. Existing tools address each substrate in isolation; no peer-reviewed protocol integrates them.

Defenses must plan for post-breach operation.

A defense taxonomy that stops at prevention is incomplete. Section 10 therefore organizes defenses not only by the lifecycle phase at which they intervene but also by whether they address pre-breach prevention, in-breach containment, or post-breach recovery—an axis that has been under-weighted in prior memory security surveys.

10. Defenses: Detection, Provenance, Recovery, and Policy

We now turn from attack surfaces to defenses. A recurring pitfall in earlier defense surveys is to organize the literature by detection technique (classifier, clustering, activation probe, perplexity filter). Such a taxonomy is convenient but systematically obscures the more important question: at which lifecycle phase does each defense intervene, and what happens if it is circumvented at that phase? In this section, we organize the literature by intervention point (the phase at which the defense acts) and breach stage (whether the defense aims at pre-breach prevention, in-breach containment, or post-breach recovery). Table 10 summarizes the resulting map; the subsequent subsections elaborate. An important methodological disclaimer up front: the joint finding of Nasr et al. (2025)—that the 12 recent prompt-injection and jailbreak defenses they evaluate are bypassed with >90%{>}90\% attack success by sufficiently adaptive attackers, despite having reported near-zero static-attack success rates—establishes, at minimum, that static robustness evaluations systematically overstate the security of defenses in this family, and the same methodological caution applies by analogy to memory defenses that have so far been evaluated only against non-adaptive baselines. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (UK National Cyber Security Centre, 2025) has taken a similar position at the policy level, arguing that prompt injection lacks the principled fix available for SQL injection and that defenders should therefore optimize for blast-radius reduction (isolation, human oversight, reversibility) rather than expect a silver bullet. We therefore flag, for each defense, what it can accomplish and what it cannot yet demonstrably accomplish under adaptive evaluation, and we treat defenses that bound the consequences of an unavoidable compromise as at least as important as those that aim to prevent it.

10.1. Write-Time Defenses: Pre-Consolidation Validation

The foundational claim of Section 4 was that memory writes should be treated as privileged state transitions requiring validation. This position is now being realized in two complementary directions.

First, human-verified freezing. VerificAgent (Nguyen et al., 2025) (Tier-2) treats persistent memory verification as a scalable-oversight problem: an LLM agent drafts candidate memory entries, these are routed through a human-verifiable audit, and only entries that pass are committed to a “frozen safety contract.” The paper reports that the generate-then-freeze pipeline blocks a substantial fraction of injection attempts under the Red-Team Memory Injection (RTMI) testbed it introduces; the precise numbers should be read as initial evidence pending peer review. The conceptual contribution is that write-time validation is not merely a filter but a contract: the set of memories the system is committed to holding as authoritative is bounded by what the human or policy authority has explicitly accepted.

Second, provenance-bearing writes. The MemCube abstraction (Li et al., 2025b) attaches source, version, sensitivity, and temporal metadata to each memory unit at write time. Provenance alone is not a filter, but it is a precondition for many downstream defenses: metadata-gated retrieval, scope-aware sharing, and cross-substrate deletion all require that the entry carry traceable lineage from its creation.

A concrete engineering instantiation of pre-consolidation validation decomposes the write gate into four components: (i) role-attribution gating—strict code-level enforcement that only content whose source role is user may be committed as a fact about the user, preventing the system from internalizing its own outputs as user experience; (ii) instruction-content filtering—scanning incoming text for control-flow patterns (tool calls, system-prompt overrides) before storage, so that data is committed as inert fact rather than as executable instruction; (iii) value assessment—a lightweight scorer that rejects entries with no cross-session utility (corrections, transient preferences, session-local formatting requests); and (iv) consistency checking—retrieval of semantically related existing entries to detect logical conflicts before the new entry is committed, with explicit user disambiguation when a contradiction is found. None of these components is individually novel; the combination constitutes a minimal write-gate stack whose absence explains many of the injection successes documented in Section 4.

What these defenses cannot yet claim. Neither VerificAgent nor MemCube-based designs have been evaluated against adaptive write-time attackers who tailor their injection pattern to the specific validation policy in force. The analogy to Nasr et al. (2025)’s finding on prompt-injection defenses suggests caution: pre-consolidation validation should be evaluated under adaptive pressure before strong generalization claims are made.

10.2. Store-Time Defenses: Versioning, Provenance, and Compression Auditing

Store-time defense is the most under-developed part of the landscape (Section 5). What we can document here are architectural preconditions more than fielded defenses.

Versioning and snapshots.

Content-addressable snapshots and write-log auditing are necessary preconditions for rollback (Section 9.2). MemOS’s MemCube schema is compatible with such versioning; to our knowledge, however, the cross-substrate rollback protocol has not yet been exercised end-to-end in a published evaluation. We see the W3C PROV data model (Moreau et al., 2013) as the appropriate standardization point for this metadata: it already defines inter-operable structures for entities, activities, and agents, so MemCube-style schemas can adopt PROV as a serialization layer without re-inventing one.

Compression under audit thresholds.

The compression-amplification problem (Section 5.3) has no published targeted defense we are aware of. A-MemGuard (Wei et al., 2025) partially addresses it at retrieval time by detecting conflicts across related memories; the dual write-time intervention—auditing each compression/reflection step before the derived entry is admitted to a high-tier lesson memory—is a natural direction that, at present, is a design implication rather than an evaluated defense.

10.3. Retrieve-Time Defenses: From Filtering to Consensus

The retrieve phase currently hosts the densest cluster of defenses. We group them along the intuition they encode.

Certifiable robustness.

RobustRAG (Xiang et al., 2026) provides provable robustness against retrieval corruption via isolate-then-aggregate: retrieved passages are partitioned into disjoint groups, responses are generated independently, and securely aggregated. PoisonedRAG’s success drops from over 90% to roughly 10% under RobustRAG, with documented degradation on long-form generation. The certifiable property is significant—it is one of the few formally grounded defenses in the memory landscape.

Clustering and trust-aware retrieval.

TrustRAG (Zhou et al., 2025) applies K-means clustering over retrieved documents to separate benign from malicious clusters, then performs LLM self-assessment with cosine and ROUGE metrics. Recent follow-up work (Si et al., 2025) (Tier-2) extends this to semantic- and conflict-aware filtering by jointly considering content similarity and inter-passage contradictions.

Activation-based detection.

RevPRAG (Tan et al., 2025a) exploits distinct activation patterns the LLM exhibits when generating correct versus poisoned responses, reporting high true-positive rates at low false-positive rates on benchmarks; the approach requires white-box access to internal states.

Consensus-based validation.

A-MemGuard (Wei et al., 2025) (Tier-2) is, by our reading, the most memory-native retrieval-phase defense published to date. Rather than classifying a single retrieved entry in isolation, it retrieves a set of semantically related memories, generates independent reasoning paths from each, and treats inter-path disagreement as an anomaly signal. Detected attacks are distilled into a “lesson memory” used to harden future decisions. Two observations in the paper bear directly on the broader landscape: (i) even strong LLM detectors miss a substantial fraction of poisoned entries in isolation, because the poisoned content does not become suspicious until it is placed in conflict with other memories; and (ii) memory attacks can cause self-reinforcing error loops that raise the attack surface for later incidents.

Realism of existing evaluations.

A Tier-2 study on memory poisoning attack and defense (Sunil et al., 2026) reports that when pre-existing legitimate memories are present in the store, the effectiveness of strong attacks such as MINJA drops substantially compared with idealized experimental conditions, and proposes composite trust scoring, memory sanitization, and trust-aware retrieval as practical countermeasures. The implication is not that prior reports are wrong—they are correct within their threat models—but that evaluation realism matters: attack success rates measured in empty-memory conditions should be interpreted as upper bounds rather than as expected deployed performance.

10.4. Execute-Time Defenses: Information-Flow Control

If retrieve-time defenses ask what is admitted to the context window, execute-time defenses ask what the model is allowed to do with it.

CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2025) is representative: it explicitly extracts control and data flows from trusted queries and enforces that untrusted data cannot influence the program flow. The paper reports that CaMeL solves 77% of tasks with provable security on the AgentDojo benchmark, a substantial number given the strength of the guarantee. FIDES (Costa et al., 2025) and PCAS (Palumbo et al., 2026) (Tier-2) extend the information-flow-control direction with richer label systems and Datalog-derived policy enforcement. Three further proposals harden execute-time defenses from different angles. Progent (Shi et al., 2025) (Tier-2) introduces a domain-specific language for fine-grained per-tool-call privilege policies and, with hand-authored policies, reportedly drives the attack success rate on Agent Security Bench to near zero; the open question is how much of that result depends on policy authorship effort. IsolateGPT (Wu et al., 2025b) proposes a hub-and-spoke execution-isolation architecture that confines each third-party application’s access to user data and tools to an enclave, preventing cross-context leakage at modest (<30%{<}30\%) overhead. Type-directed privilege separation (Jacob et al., 2025) (Tier-2) decomposes an agent into a quarantined data-handling component and a privileged control component, restricting the data the privileged component may consume to closed-form types (booleans, enums, small structs); the authors argue this eliminates prompt-injection-style control-flow hijacking in a type-theoretic sense. Together, these are representative of a shift from post-hoc filtering to architectural execute-time defense, consistent with the blast-radius framing of UK National Cyber Security Centre (2025).

Complementing IFC, contextualized privacy defense (Wen et al., 2026) (Tier-2) injects step-specific privacy guidance at execution time via an instructor model, reportedly obtaining better privacy–helpfulness trade-offs than static guardrails. This is particularly useful because many execute-time failures are context-sensitive: what counts as a privacy violation in a healthcare tool call differs from what counts in a public-information lookup.

The principal limitation of this family, at present, is coverage: IFC tools have been evaluated primarily on static tool suites and on relatively constrained threat models. Their behavior under memory-driven control-flow attacks such as MCFA (Xu et al., 2026) is an open empirical question.

10.5. Share-Time Defenses: Principal-Scoped Policy

The share phase—where contagion and leakage occur—requires defenses that reason about principals, not just content. Collaborative Memory (Rezazadeh et al., 2025) formalizes this by encoding access policies as a time-evolving bipartite graph over principals, agents, and resources; it is the most developed published framework we are aware of for multi-user, multi-agent memory. Recent preprint work on agent access control (Li et al., 2025a) advocates moving from binary allow/deny permissions to dynamic information-flow governance, consistent with the arguments from Section 7.1 and the CaMeL/FIDES direction. A complementary direction is unsupervised anomaly detection on multi-agent interaction graphs. Miao et al. (2025) (BlindGuard, Tier-2) train a hierarchical agent-level encoder using only normal trajectories and flag deviations at the node, neighbourhood, and graph levels; because it does not require labelled attacks, BlindGuard generalizes to the kind of previously unseen multi-agent contagion patterns documented in Section 7.2.

From the benign side, the unintentional cross-user contamination (UCC) study (Yang et al., 2026) (Tier-2) makes clear that share-phase defenses must contend with non-adversarial failure modes: even in the absence of any attacker, 57–71% of benign interactions yielded cross-user contamination in the reported experiments, and text sanitization alone was inadequate for executable artifacts. This motivates pairing principal-scoped policy with scope-correctness invariants that are enforceable even on legitimate writes.

10.6. Post-Breach Defenses: Forensics and Recovery

Post-breach defense is the thinnest layer in the current landscape, but also the one whose absence most directly undermines governance. RAGForensics (Zhang et al., 2025c) (WWW 2025) demonstrates that systematic post-hoc traceback is feasible on static RAG corpora: given a detected attack, the system iteratively retrieves text subsets and uses crafted prompts to localize the poisoned entries responsible. Its limitation is that agent memory is not a static corpus; extending RAGForensics-style traceback across the Write, Store, and Retrieve phases of an evolving memory store is, to our knowledge, an open engineering and research problem.

Industry-side, the OWASP Agent Memory Guard project (OWASP Foundation, 2026a) (Tier-3) provides an initial reference implementation covering hashing-based integrity baselines, policy enforcement, and snapshot/rollback primitives. It should be read as a community signal that these primitives are expected of production systems, rather than as an evaluated research artifact; but the existence of a community reference is itself evidence that the industry now treats post-breach recovery for memory as a first-class concern.

10.7. What Defenses Do Not Yet Provide

Three gaps are visible in Table 10 and the discussion above.

First, cross-phase composition is not yet studied. Most defenses target a single phase; very little work examines how defenses at different phases compose, whether their guarantees interact adversarially, or how attacks reroute around a single-phase defense by exploiting upstream or downstream phases.

Second, benchmarks are partial. Agent Security Bench (Zhang et al., 2025a) and AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024) offer partial coverage of prompt injection and memory-poisoning scenarios; the RAG-poisoning-specific RSB (Zhang et al., 2025d) covers many attacks and defenses on retrieval corpora; and capability-oriented benchmarks such as MemBench (Tan et al., 2025b), LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025c), LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024), and MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2026) measure how well agents use their memory—but without a security axis. What is missing is a benchmark that explicitly spans the full lifecycle and the full objective matrix—covering, at minimum, write-time injection, store-time retention and audit, retrieval-phase corruption, execute-time control-flow capture, share-phase contagion, and forget-phase rollback under realistic conditions—and that joins the security and capability axes in a single evaluation. Table 11 summarises current coverage along these axes and makes the joint gap explicit.

Third, post-breach recovery is under-tested. No peer-reviewed evaluation we are aware of reports end-to-end rollback and forensic traceback on a dynamically written agent memory store, with verified deletion semantics. Until such evaluations exist, claims about mnemonic sovereignty remain partially architectural.

Fourth, adaptive evaluation is absent for memory-specific defenses. Nasr et al. (2025) demonstrated that 12 recent prompt-injection and jailbreak defenses that reported near-zero static-attack success rates are bypassed with >90%{>}90\% success by sufficiently adaptive attackers. By analogy, every memory defense surveyed above—pre-consolidation validation, trust-aware retrieval, consensus-based detection, IFC enforcement—has been evaluated only against non-adaptive or weakly adaptive attack suites. We do not claim these defenses are therefore broken; we claim that their security margins are unknown under the standard that mature security evaluation demands. To close this gap, future evaluation should follow the Nasr et al. (2025) methodology: given a specific defense configuration, construct an attacker that is granted knowledge of the defense mechanism and allowed to optimize against it, and report the resulting attack success rate alongside the non-adaptive baseline. Until such evaluations are conducted, defense effectiveness claims in the memory-security literature should be read as lower bounds on the effort required for attack, not as robust security guarantees.

Fifth, governance overhead is empirically uncosted. Provenance metadata, version snapshots, audit logs, and per-write policy evaluation all impose storage, latency, and compute costs that no published study has systematically measured for agent memory stores. Wolff and Bennati (2026) provide early evidence that even capability-focused memory operations carry non-trivial resource costs; governance metadata can only increase that baseline. Without cost data, it is difficult to assess the practical deployability of the governance-first designs advocated in this survey.

These gaps structure the research agenda in Section 12.

11. Memory System Architectures as Determinants of Governability

Architectures determine which lifecycle phases are explicitly governable. A system that exposes only writes and retrievals cannot, in principle, support the provenance, versioning, and principal-scoped access policies that the preceding sections argue are necessary for mnemonic sovereignty. This section compares representative architectures along the primitives the lifecycle framework requires, with the aim not of ranking systems or declaring commercial “winners,” but of identifying which lifecycle phases each architecture makes governable.

We include six architectures that span the current design space: MemGPT (virtual memory hierarchy), MemoryBank (forgetting-curve retention), Mem0 (production-oriented long-term memory), MemOS (memory-as-resource operating system), Collaborative Memory (multi-user access control), and CoALA (cognitive-architecture framing). Each system has its own design goals; our comparison asks only which governance primitives its published architecture makes available.

11.1. Architectural Primitives for Mnemonic Sovereignty

From the preceding sections we distill nine primitives a memory architecture should expose if it is to support full-lifecycle governance:

  1. P1.

    Memory unit abstraction. Is each memory entry a first-class object with identity, or merely a text fragment in a store?

  2. P2.

    Write gate. Does the architecture expose a hook for pre-consolidation validation before content is committed?

  3. P3.

    Provenance metadata. Source, principal, and context fields attached at write time.

  4. P4.

    Versioning. Are snapshots, write logs, or content-addressable diffs available?

  5. P5.

    Trust / sensitivity labels. Can entries carry labels that downstream retrieval and execution policies can read?

  6. P6.

    Principal scoping. Does the retrieval layer respect per-principal boundaries, or is the store globally queryable?

  7. P7.

    Rollback. Can the system return to a prior memory state after a detected incident?

  8. P8.

    Deletion semantics. Does the architecture specify what a deletion operation propagates to (raw log, summaries, indices, derived lessons)?

  9. P9.

    Internal-channel observability. Are inter-agent messages, tool-call arguments, and shared-state reads recorded as first-class observable events?

These primitives operationalize the mnemonic-sovereignty concept of Section 2.4: a system that exposes all nine can, in principle, enforce integrity, confidentiality, availability, and governance across the lifecycle; a system that exposes only the first three cannot. Primitives P3–P9 are, with minor additions, expressible in the W3C PROV Data Model (Moreau et al., 2013), which already standardizes entities, activities, agents, and derivations. An implementation that treats PROV as its metadata serialization thus starts from an interoperable baseline rather than a bespoke schema; this is the lightest-weight step we are aware of toward governance by construction.

11.2. A Comparison Matrix

Table 12 compares the six architectures against the nine primitives. Cells report the status of the primitive as explicit in the published architecture (✓), partial / implicit (⚫), or not reported (✗). This is an assessment of the published architecture descriptions, not of deployed implementations, which may have evolved past their descriptions. Figure 6 renders the same data as overlapping polygons on a nine-axis radar, making it easy to see which primitives are broadly covered (P1, P3) and which remain collective blind spots (notably P2, the write gate, where no published architecture reaches explicit support).

Four observations bear discussion.

No published architecture is full-spectrum.

No row in Table 12 is entirely ✓. MemOS and Collaborative Memory cover the most primitives in their published descriptions, but even they have partial or unreported primitives—most notably around post-deletion verification, compression-lineage preservation, and adversarial rollback evaluation. Two caveats apply. First, architectural exposure does not equal security effectiveness: neither MemOS nor Collaborative Memory has published adversarial evaluations demonstrating that these mechanisms withstand the attacks catalogued in Sections 4–7. Second, architectures that score lower on Table 12 (e.g., MemGPT, Mem0) were designed with capability and efficiency—not governance—as their primary objective; a lower governance score does not imply an inferior architecture for their intended use cases. Accordingly, this table should be read as a governance-gap diagnostic, not as an overall capability ranking among competing systems.

Virtual-memory architectures prioritize capability and efficiency.

MemGPT’s tier hierarchy (Packer et al., 2023) and Mem0’s production design (Chhikara et al., 2025) have demonstrated strong capability gains—Mem0 reports a 26% judge-metric improvement over baseline global memory, with a 91% latency reduction and 90%+ token-cost savings on LOCOMO—and their designs were not intended to address governance as a primary objective. In a security-centered analysis, they provide essential infrastructure that future governance layers can build upon.

Metadata-bearing “memory-as-resource” designs expose more governance primitives than retrieval-only stores.

Architectures that attach structured metadata to each memory unit expose a richer surface for governance than retrieval-only stores. MemOS’s MemCube abstraction (Li et al., 2025b) is one instantiation of this design pattern: it attaches source, version, timestamp, and sensitivity metadata to each memory unit, and its MemScheduler infrastructure offers a natural hook for policy enforcement. This reading, however, is about the design pattern, not about any single product: any architecture whose metadata model is comparably expressive (e.g., a PROV-conformant serialization (Moreau et al., 2013) or the emerging harness-level metadata models of ClawVM (Rafique and Bindschaedler, 2026)) would appear in the same region of Table 12. What metadata-bearing designs do provide is the structural layer required for provenance-gated retrieval, versioned rollback, and scope-aware access control—primitives that retrieval-only stores such as MemoryBank or CoALA do not expose by construction. What they do not yet provide is adversarial evidence that these mechanisms withstand the attacks documented in Sections 4–7. MemOS specifically has not published adversarial red-team evaluations, nor a quantitative comparison of its governance overhead against capability-focused baselines such as Mem0-style deployments; closing these gaps is among the more important empirical directions for memory-architecture research and a precondition for any strong claim about governance readiness.

Multi-user and cognitive-architecture framings bring orthogonal contributions.

Collaborative Memory (Rezazadeh et al., 2025) adds the principal-scoping and access-graph infrastructure necessary for multi-user deployments; CoALA (Sumers et al., 2024) does not advance the governance primitives but provides an important decompositional vocabulary (long-term vs. working vs. episodic vs. procedural memory; decision-action loops) that makes it easier to locate which memory substrate each concrete defense should be applied to. These contributions are not substitutes for metadata-bearing architectures; they are complementary substrates that a governance-first design should be able to compose.

11.3. Toward Governance-First Memory Architectures

Reading Table 12 through the sovereign-memory lens suggests a concrete design programme for next-generation architectures. We name four principles that, in our judgment, a governance-first memory architecture should embody.

First, treat every write as a typed state transition, with provenance, principal, context, and sensitivity attached at the moment of ingestion. VerificAgent-style freezing (Nguyen et al., 2025) and MemCube-style metadata (Li et al., 2025b) are partial precedents.

Second, preserve compression lineage. Whenever a summary or lesson is derived from raw entries, the derivation must remain traceable. This is the most commonly absent primitive across Table 12.

Third, treat principal scope as first-class retrieval state. A retrieval policy that cannot express “entries readable by principal AA but not derivable by principal BB” is insufficient for multi-user deployments, independent of any adversarial concern (Rezazadeh et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a).

Fourth, make forgetting verifiable, not best-effort. Deletion should be accompanied by an audit-verifiable protocol that propagates across raw logs, summaries, indices, and—where relevant and technically feasible—parametric substrates. At present, we know of no peer-reviewed architecture that demonstrates this end-to-end. This is arguably the largest open problem at the architecture-governance boundary and a focus of Section 12.

None of these principles are esoteric; each maps directly to well-established concepts in systems security (typed writes, information-flow provenance, scope-aware access control, verifiable deletion). Their absence in most current memory architectures reflects an implicit assumption, inherited from the early days of retrieval-augmented generation, that memory is a cache—a helpful piece of infrastructure whose integrity is not mission-critical. The evidence assembled in this survey argues the opposite: memory is the substrate through which an agent’s past governs its future behavior, and the architectures that host it must be designed accordingly.

Three recent prototypes illustrate that this programme is beginning to crystallize into concrete systems. SSGM (Lam et al., 2026) explicitly frames the governance of evolving memory as its organizing problem: it composes pre-consolidation validation, temporal and provenance grounding, access-scoped retrieval, and reversible reconciliation into a single memory lifecycle, and is—to our knowledge—the first architecture whose contribution is articulated primarily in governance, rather than capability, terms. ClawVM (Rafique and Bindschaedler, 2026) approaches the same goal from the systems side: it models agent memory as harness-managed virtual memory with typed pages, minimum-fidelity invariants, and validated writeback, and makes the harness itself a deterministic enforcement point for lifecycle policy. MemMachine (Wang et al., 2026c), by contrast, attacks the compression-lineage gap directly: rather than distilling episodes into lossy summaries at write time, it retains ground-truth episodes and performs contextualized retrieval at query time, which, if the reported properties hold under adversarial study, would mitigate a large fraction of the compression-amplification pathway described in Section 5. None of the three is a complete mnemonic-sovereignty substrate; together, they show that governance-first, harness-typed, and lineage-preserving are emerging as three complementary—and, so far, largely independent—architectural strategies.

11.4. The Agent Harness as a Governance Substrate

A growing body of systems work suggests that memory governance cannot be fully understood at the memory-module level alone. The agent harness—the runtime layer that assembles prompts, mediates tool calls, manages compaction and flushes, and emits lifecycle events—has begun to emerge as a first-class governance substrate in its own right.

Zhou et al. (2026) frame the recent evolution of agent systems as a progression from weights to context to harness, positioning harness engineering as the unification layer that coordinates externalized memory, skills, and protocols. ClawVM (Rafique and Bindschaedler, 2026) instantiates this view by applying OS-style virtual memory (page tables, fault observers, writeback journals) at the harness layer, making state residency and durability deterministic and auditable. Natural-Language Agent Harnesses (Pan et al., 2026) go further, proposing that harness behavior itself be expressed in editable natural language and executed through explicit contracts and durable artifacts. On the enforcement side, AgentSpec (Wang et al., 2026a) (ICSE 2026) provides a lightweight DSL for specifying trigger–predicate–enforcement rules that a runtime framework applies with millisecond-level overhead.

For memory security specifically, these developments imply that several sovereignty primitives—especially write gating (P2), rollback (P7), deletion propagation (P8), and internal-channel observability (P9)—may be more naturally implemented at the harness level than inside the memory store. At the same time, the harness is not a semantic oracle: provenance semantics (P3), trust attribution (P5), and content-level truth verification still require memory metadata and model- or policy-level validation. Future benchmarks should therefore test not only memory-module behavior in isolation but also harness-level lifecycle enforcement under adversarial conditions.

12. Research Agenda Toward Mnemonic Sovereignty

The preceding ten sections have mapped an attack-dominant landscape in which defenses are advancing but remain partial, architectures expose fewer governance primitives than the lifecycle framework requires, and evaluation benchmarks cover only a subset of the phases. We now turn from description to prescription. This section organizes the open problems into a research agenda structured around three arguments. First, mnemonic sovereignty is useful only if it can be operationalized; we propose a concrete primitive-plus-metric framework for doing so. Second, the field needs a broader notion of risk that does not reduce to malicious adversaries. Third, a distinct line of research—LLM-as-tool in memory security—is currently sparse and merits focused development.

12.1. Operationalizing Mnemonic Sovereignty

Throughout this survey we have used mnemonic sovereignty as a normative umbrella for integrity, confidentiality, availability, and governance of agent memory (Sections 2.4, 3.3, 11.1). Section 11.1 introduced nine architectural support primitives (P1–P9) that describe what a memory system can expose—the building blocks an architecture may or may not implement. Here we shift from architectural description to normative evaluation: we distill five testable sovereignty primitives that specify what a system must demonstrate to justify a governance claim. The five are a focused subset: they draw on the nine architectural primitives but select and compose those that are most directly evaluable. For each, we pair an architectural substrate, a representative threat it must withstand, a representative defense direction, and a proposed evaluation metric. Table 13 summarizes the proposal. We do not claim these five primitives exhaust the space; rather, we claim they are the minimum set a system must pass to justify a sovereignty claim.

Several properties of Table 13 are worth emphasizing. The five primitives are not independent: verified forgetting depends on rollbackability, which in turn depends on provenance visibility, which in turn depends on write authorization. A system that omits any earlier primitive cannot meaningfully claim the later ones, regardless of how sophisticated its deletion interface appears to end users. Figure 7 renders this dependency as a tower: the widest, most mature foundation is write authorization; each successive layer narrows and becomes less deployed; the crowning primitive—verified forgetting—currently has no peer-reviewed end-to-end instantiation.

A candid assessment of the dependency chain.

The dependency structure 𝖵𝖥⪯𝖱𝖡⪯𝖯𝖵⪯𝖶𝖠\mathsf{VF}\preceq\mathsf{RB}\preceq\mathsf{PV}\preceq\mathsf{WA} is a design pre-order: it states that implementing a higher-level primitive architecturally requires the lower ones. This is a logical implication, not a circular definition—the dependency is linear, not reflexive. However, the practical consequence is sobering. Provenance visibility (PV), the foundation for rollback and verified forgetting, is currently rare in published architectures (Table 12 shows only two systems with explicit provenance metadata). This means the upper layers of the tower rest on an infrastructure that is, at present, largely aspirational. We do not regard this as an objection to the framework; rather, it is the central diagnostic the framework provides: the maturity gradient in Figure 7 is not a minor inconvenience but a structural gap the field must close. Concretely, this means that near-term progress toward mnemonic sovereignty should prioritize provenance infrastructure (P3–P5 in Table 12) over higher-level primitives whose preconditions do not yet exist in most systems.

Formal definition.

To make the five primitives amenable to evaluation rather than mere discussion, we cast them as predicates over a memory store MtM_{t} at time tt. Let each entry m∈Mtm\in M_{t} carry metadata (src⁡(m),scope⁡(m),prov⁡(m),ver⁡(m))(\operatorname{src}(m),\,\operatorname{scope}(m),\,\operatorname{prov}(m),\,\operatorname{ver}(m)), denoting the source principal, authorized principal set, provenance record, and version identifier, respectively. The five primitives are then:

(1) 𝖶𝖠⁡(Mt)\displaystyle\mathsf{WA}(M_{t}) :=∀m∈Mt,src(m)≠⊥∧𝖺𝗎𝗍𝗁W(src(m),m,t)=1,\displaystyle:=\forall m\!\in\!M_{t},\;\operatorname{src}(m)\neq\bot\;\land\;\mathsf{auth}_{W}\!\bigl(\operatorname{src}(m),m,t\bigr)=1,
