(2) 𝖯𝖵⁡(Mt)\displaystyle\mathsf{PV}(M_{t}) :=∀m∈Mt,prov⁡(m)​ is queryable and lineage-complete,\displaystyle:=\forall m\!\in\!M_{t},\;\operatorname{prov}(m)\text{ is queryable and lineage-complete},
(3) 𝖯𝖲⁡(Mt)\displaystyle\mathsf{PS}(M_{t}) :=∀q,π,R⁡(q,π,Mt)⊆{m∈Mt:π∈scope⁡(m)},\displaystyle:=\forall q,\pi,\;R(q,\pi,M_{t})\subseteq\{m\!\in\!M_{t}:\pi\!\in\!\operatorname{scope}(m)\},
(4) 𝖱𝖡⁡(Mt)\displaystyle\mathsf{RB}(M_{t}) :=∃t0<t​s.t.​𝗋𝗈𝗅𝗅𝖻𝖺𝖼𝗄​(Mt,t0)=Mt0,\displaystyle:=\exists\,t_{0}\!<\!t\;\text{s.t.}\;\mathsf{rollback}(M_{t},t_{0})=M_{t_{0}},
(5) 𝖵𝖥ε​(Mt)\displaystyle\mathsf{VF}_{\varepsilon}(M_{t}) :=∀X,Prq∼QX[ExposeX(q,FX(Mt))=1]≤ε.\displaystyle:=\forall X,\;\Pr\nolimits_{q\sim Q_{X}}\!\bigl[\operatorname{Expose}_{X}\!\bigl(q,\,F_{X}(M_{t})\bigr)=1\bigr]\leq\varepsilon.

A system satisfies ε\varepsilon-mnemonic sovereignty at time tt if all five hold simultaneously:

(6) 𝖬𝖲ε​(Mt):=𝖶𝖠⁡(Mt)∧𝖯𝖵⁡(Mt)∧𝖯𝖲⁡(Mt)∧𝖱𝖡⁡(Mt)∧𝖵𝖥ε​(Mt).\mathsf{MS}_{\varepsilon}(M_{t})\;:=\;\mathsf{WA}(M_{t})\;\land\;\mathsf{PV}(M_{t})\;\land\;\mathsf{PS}(M_{t})\;\land\;\mathsf{RB}(M_{t})\;\land\;\mathsf{VF}_{\varepsilon}(M_{t}).

The dependency tower of Figure 7 can now be stated as a design pre-order: under lineage-based deletion,

(7) 𝖵𝖥ε⪯𝖱𝖡⪯𝖯𝖵⪯𝖶𝖠,\mathsf{VF}_{\varepsilon}\preceq\mathsf{RB}\preceq\mathsf{PV}\preceq\mathsf{WA},

where X⪯YX\preceq Y means that implementing XX requires YY as an architectural precondition. Principal-scoped retrieval (𝖯𝖲\mathsf{PS}) is orthogonal to this lineage chain but necessary for any confidentiality claim. This dependency structure is the clearest reason that mnemonic sovereignty is a lifecycle property: it cannot be added as a final layer.

Limitations of the 𝖵𝖥ε\mathsf{VF}_{\varepsilon} formulation.

The verified-forgetting predicate (5) assumes access to a membership oracle ExposeX\operatorname{Expose}_{X} that can detect whether a deleted entry XX still influences the memory store. Two practical difficulties deserve explicit acknowledgement. First, for derivative entries—summaries, reflections, or lessons produced by compression pipelines (Section 5.3)—the notion of “reappearance of XX” is semantically fuzzy: a summary SS that was derived from XX together with entries Y1,…,YkY_{1},\ldots,Y_{k} may retain partial influence of XX without reproducing XX verbatim, and quantifying that partial influence is itself an open problem. Second, when derivative chains are deep (e.g., a summary SS that influenced a subsequent reflection TT), deletion of XX requires a causal dependency graph to determine which downstream entries must also be invalidated. Constructing and maintaining such a graph is precisely what the provenance-visibility primitive (𝖯𝖵\mathsf{PV}) is meant to support, but the absence of 𝖯𝖵\mathsf{PV} in most current architectures means that 𝖵𝖥ε\mathsf{VF}_{\varepsilon} is, at present, a formal aspiration rather than a testable property. We include the formalization nonetheless because it makes the gap precise and thereby helps direct future work toward formal causal-dependency models for memory deletion.

Table 13 also has a natural reading through established risk-management frameworks. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023) organizes AI governance around four core functions—Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage—and our five primitives project onto them straightforwardly: write authorization and principal-scoped retrieval realize the Govern and Map functions (who can commit what, in which scope); provenance visibility realizes Map and Measure; rollbackability realizes Manage; and verified forgetting realizes Measure and Manage simultaneously, because the deletion primitive is only meaningful if its effect can be verified. We therefore see the primitives not as a competitor to AI RMF but as a memory-specific refinement of its Map/Measure/Manage loop. Emerging regulatory requirements reinforce this connection: if deployer strict-liability frameworks (as anticipated under the EU Product Liability Directive and AI Act record-keeping obligations) become the norm, memory systems will need tamper-evident write logs, externally auditable memory diffs, and non-repudiable deletion proofs as minimum architectural properties—requirements that no published system currently satisfies end-to-end.

12.2. Risk Without an Attacker: The Benign-Persistence Axis

A conventional security survey would stop with adversarial threats. The evidence assembled in this survey supports a stronger claim: some of the most consequential memory-security failures do not require an attacker at all. Four lines of work converge on this point.

First, Zhang et al. (2024b) (Tier-2) report that users are typically unaware of what their memory-augmented system retains, cannot accurately predict its contents, and do not know how to effectively delete it. This is a confidentiality failure mediated entirely by benign persistence.

Second, the unintentional cross-user contamination study, Yang et al. (2026) (Tier-2), reports that 57–71% of benign interactions in shared-state agents produce cross-user contamination, with text-level sanitization insufficient for executable artifacts. The contaminant is not malicious; the failure is a scoping failure.

Third, preliminary work on context-aware preference selectivity (Yoon et al., 2026) (Tier-2) indicates that stronger preference adherence in persistent profile memory can produce higher rates of over-application: the agent applies the user’s preference in contexts where it is institutionally inappropriate (e.g., in a third-party communication). The memory is correct; the context is wrong. At the attack-evaluation side, PS-Bench (Guo et al., 2026) (Tier-2) reports that the presence of benign personalized memory raises the attack success rate of standard dialogue jailbreaks by 15.8%–243.7% versus a memoryless baseline: benign memory legitimizes harmful intent inferences the agent would otherwise reject, a phenomenon Guo et al. name intent legitimation. The attacker in PS-Bench is adversarial, but the amplification channel is benign persistence, which is why we locate the finding on this axis rather than on the adversarial one.

Fourth, work on when persistent memory should forget (Pulipaka et al., 2026) (Tier-2) reports high rates of memory-induced sycophancy and cross-domain leakage across many frontier models. These are not attacker-induced failures; they are properties of over-retentive systems.

Crucially, these four studies span different lifecycle phases: retention awareness at Store (Zhang et al., 2024b), write-time scoping at Share (Yang et al., 2026), retrieve-time context matching (Yoon et al., 2026), and execute-time safety amplification (Guo et al., 2026). This distribution suggests that benign-persistence failures are not confined to a single phase but track the lifecycle in a manner parallel to adversarial threats—reinforcing the case for lifecycle-wide analysis rather than phase-specific treatment.

Together, these findings support treating benign persistence, scope mismatch, and context misapplication as first-class memory-security threats. A research agenda that addresses only malicious adversaries would leave a substantial portion of real-world failure modes outside its scope. We do not claim the benign axis is better studied than the adversarial one—it is, in fact, considerably less so. But the evidence is sufficient to justify its being surveyed as a distinct track going forward, and we recommend that future benchmarks include non-adversarial scenarios alongside adversarial ones.

12.3. Area 2: LLM-Driven Memory Security (LLM-as-Tool)

A second under-developed track concerns the use of LLMs themselves as tools for attacking or defending memory systems. We name it Area 2 in deliberate contrast to the main body of this survey (Area 1: attacks on and defenses of memory systems), and we flag it as one of the largest gaps visible in the literature as of writing.

LLM as memory defender.

The clearest existing example is A-MemGuard (Wei et al., 2025) (Section 10.3), which uses LLM reasoning to generate independent paths from related memories and flags inter-path disagreement as an anomaly. VerificAgent (Nguyen et al., 2025) uses an LLM to draft candidate memory entries that a human or policy authority then freezes. Beyond these two works, systematic investigation of LLM-driven memory defense—including write-time semantic audit, cross-session consistency detection over memory snapshots, and LLM-based synthesis of plausible counterfactual memories for stress-testing—is sparse.

LLM as memory attacker.

InjecMEM (Tian et al., 2026) and MINJA (Dong et al., 2025) both leverage LLM reasoning in their attack construction (Multi-GCG optimization; bridging steps and indication prompts), but there is not yet a systematic treatment of LLMs as automated red-team generators for memory systems. General-purpose LLM-vs-LLM jailbreak frameworks such as Russinovich et al. (2025) operate on single sessions and have not been adapted, to our knowledge, to persistent-memory settings.

LLM as automated memory red-teamer.

The analogous tool for memory red-teaming would be a pipeline in which an attacker LLM iteratively probes the boundaries of an agent’s memory write gate, retrieval key space, and reflection policy, while a scoring model evaluates the resulting state transitions. No such pipeline is available in the published literature at the time of writing. Developing one is, in our judgment, the single highest-leverage research direction within Area 2: it would turn the evaluation of memory-specific defenses from ad-hoc testing into a reproducible, scalable procedure.

Why Area 2 matters.

The motivation for this track is not novelty but necessity. Memory defenses that have not been evaluated under adaptive LLM red-teaming cannot be trusted at the levels of rigor that Nasr et al. (2025) established for prompt-injection defense. Area 2 is the infrastructure that Area 1’s defenses require if they are to earn credibility comparable to mature security fields.

12.4. Cross-Phase Composition and Lifecycle-Wide Benchmarks

A structural observation from Sections 10 and 11 is that defenses and architectures are typically evaluated at a single lifecycle phase. Very little is known about how defenses compose, or how attacks reroute around a single-phase defense by exploiting upstream or downstream phases.

A concrete scenario illustrates the risk. Suppose a Write-phase validator correctly identifies overt injection attempts but admits a borderline observation—for example, a user preference phrased as “always use the admin API endpoint for deploy commands.” At the Store phase, compression or reflection distills this into a high-level procedural rule, stripping the conversational context that would flag it as externally planted. When the Retrieve phase later surfaces the rule, its provenance metadata has been diluted by the compression step, so retrieval-time consensus or anomaly detection treats it as a well-established preference rather than a single-source insertion. Finally, at the Execute phase, an IFC policy that restricts direct tool calls cannot block the poisoned plan, because the instruction arrives as a “remembered preference” rather than a runtime injection. Each single-phase defense behaves correctly in isolation; the vulnerability emerges only from their composition across the lifecycle.

We identify three concrete open problems in this direction.

P1: Composable defense semantics.

Can we give formal guarantees for the composition of a Write-phase validation, a Retrieve-phase consensus check, and an Execute-phase IFC policy? At present, each of these is evaluated in isolation, and the joint failure modes are unstudied. A minimal measurable quantity is the non-compositionality gap. Let ηi∈[0,1]\eta_{i}\!\in\![0,1] be the phase-local efficacy of defense DiD_{i} (the fractional reduction it induces on the corresponding conditional failure probability). Under an independence assumption, the expected joint efficacy is ηind=1−∏i(1−ηi)\eta_{\mathrm{ind}}=1-\prod_{i}(1-\eta_{i}). If the observed end-to-end efficacy under simultaneous deployment is ηjoint=1−PcompD1,…,Dk/Pcomp\eta_{\mathrm{joint}}=1-P_{\mathrm{comp}}^{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}}/P_{\mathrm{comp}}, then Δcomp:=ηjoint−ηind\Delta_{\mathrm{comp}}:=\eta_{\mathrm{joint}}-\eta_{\mathrm{ind}} quantifies synergy (Δcomp>0\Delta_{\mathrm{comp}}\!>\!0) or interference (Δcomp<0\Delta_{\mathrm{comp}}\!<\!0) across lifecycle phases. A negative gap is plausible when store-time compression strips away provenance needed by a retrieve-time consensus check, or when an execute-time IFC policy is bypassed because the harmful instruction arrives as remembered state rather than runtime input.

P2: Lifecycle-wide benchmark.

Agent Security Bench (Zhang et al., 2025a), AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024), and RSB (Zhang et al., 2025d) offer partial coverage of prompt injection, tool misuse, and RAG poisoning. InjecAgent (Zhan et al., 2024) additionally benchmarks indirect prompt injection in tool-integrated agents, and AgentHarm (Andriushchenko et al., 2025) measures harmful-task compliance of agent stacks under jailbreaks; both live on the execute–share axis rather than spanning the lifecycle. On the memory-capability side, LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025c) (ICLR 2025), LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) (ACL 2024), Minerva (Xia et al., 2025) (ICML 2025), and MemoryCD (Zhang et al., 2026) (Tier-2) assess extraction, multi-session reasoning, programmable atomic memory operations, and cross-domain lifelong personalization, respectively. MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2026) takes a step in the lifecycle direction on the capability side. What is still missing is a benchmark that explicitly spans the full six phases and the full objective matrix—covering write-time injection, store-time retention and audit, retrieve-phase corruption, execute-time control-flow capture, share-phase contagion, and forget-phase rollback—by composing these capability benchmarks with adversarial conditions drawn from ASB, InjecAgent, and RSB.

P3: Post-breach evaluation.

Current benchmarks evaluate defenses in steady state: does the system resist an attack introduced against a known-safe baseline? Post-breach evaluation asks the complementary question: given that a poisoning has succeeded, can the system detect it, trace it, roll back to a safe state, and verify remediation? No peer-reviewed benchmark, to our knowledge, systematically measures these post-breach capabilities. This is consistent with our finding (Table 12) that Forget/Rollback primitives are the least-implemented across published architectures.

P4: Memory lineage attribution.

In agentic workflows where memories evolve autonomously—through reflection, compression, or inter-agent sharing—a single memory entry may have passed through NN transformation hops before it influences a downstream action. When that action causes harm, the system should be able to identify which hop introduced the deviation. No existing benchmark tests this capability; current evaluations (Table 11) assume a single injection point rather than a lineage graph. Designing such an attribution benchmark, and the provenance infrastructure it presupposes, is a prerequisite for any serious accountability framework.

12.5. Architectural Research Directions

Section 11 identified four design principles for governance-first memory architectures: typed writes, compression lineage, principal-scoped retrieval, and verifiable forgetting. Each maps to an open research direction.

A1: Typed-write schemas with chain-of-custody provenance.

Attaching provenance, principal, and sensitivity at every write is architecturally straightforward; doing so without unacceptable performance or storage overhead is less so. Moreover, current provenance metadata records what changed and when, but not who authorized the write, under what policy, and derived from which upstream memory entries. PROV-AGENT (Souza et al., 2025) demonstrates that W3C PROV-DM can be extended to track agent-level workflow provenance, but the granularity stops at tool calls and prompts—per-memory-write chain-of-custody remains unimplemented. This finer granularity is essential for accountability in multi-agent deployments where one agent’s memory write becomes another agent’s retrieval input. MemOS’s MemCube design is a promising substrate, but public benchmarks comparing its write-time overhead under adversarial workloads to simpler unvalidated architectures are not yet available.

A2: Compression-lineage preservation.

The cleanest formulation of this problem is: given that summary SS was derived from raw entries {r1,…,rk}\{r_{1},\dots,r_{k}\}, produce a representation that preserves the derivation cheaply and supports deletion of any rir_{i} with automatic propagation to SS. No published memory architecture solves this end-to-end. Related infrastructure (change-data-capture, materialized-view maintenance in databases) may provide technical starting points.

A3: Principal-scoped retrieval with dynamic policy.

Collaborative Memory (Rezazadeh et al., 2025) introduces the access-graph formalism; the open question is how to combine access-graph enforcement with trust-aware, provenance-aware retrieval policies in a single evaluation framework. Agent access control preprints (Li et al., 2025a) are early steps in this direction.

A4: Verified forgetting across substrates.

This is the hardest and arguably the most important architectural open problem. A candidate deletion primitive must (i) locate all derivatives of the deleted content via preserved lineage, (ii) propagate deletion across raw storage, summaries, indices, graph relations, and—where relevant—parametric substrates, and (iii) provide a verifiable certificate of deletion (e.g., membership or reappearance tests). None of these three steps is currently standard practice.

Step (iii) can be made precise. Suppose that after deleting a target content set XX, an auditor runs nn adversarial probes sampled from a query family QXQ_{X} and observes kk reappearances of XX or its derivatives. By Hoeffding’s inequality, the true reappearance probability pXp_{X} satisfies, with confidence 1−δ1-\delta,

(8) pX≤p^X+ln⁡(1/δ)2​n,p^X:=k/n.p_{X}\;\leq\;\hat{p}_{X}+\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2n}},\qquad\hat{p}_{X}:=k/n.

A sufficient condition for claiming ε\varepsilon-verified forgetting at confidence 1−δ1-\delta is therefore

p^X+ln⁡(1/δ)2​n≤ε.\hat{p}_{X}+\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2n}}\;\leq\;\varepsilon.

In the zero-failure case (k=0k=0), this reduces to n≳ln⁡(1/δ)/εn\gtrsim\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon; certifying ε=0.01\varepsilon=0.01 at 95% confidence requires n≈300n\approx 300 probes—a concrete and deployable test budget.

12.6. A Research Priority Ranking

Compressed to a single ranking, we nominate the following five directions as the highest-leverage next steps, in decreasing order of readiness to yield short-term progress:

  1. R1.

    Lifecycle-wide memory security benchmark. A benchmark covering all six phases and all four objectives, including both adversarial and benign-persistence scenarios, would immediately anchor the field and expose the composition problems identified above.

  2. R2.

    LLM-driven memory red-teaming pipeline (Area 2). Automated, adaptive attacker LLMs targeting memory write gates, retrieval policies, and reflection loops—evaluated against published defenses under the conditions of Nasr et al. (2025).

  3. R3.

    Cross-substrate verified deletion. A protocol that coordinates deletion across raw logs, summaries, retrieval indices, and (where relevant) model weights, with post-deletion verification.

  4. R4.

    Adversarial evaluation of metadata-bearing, lifecycle-managed memory architectures. Empirical stress-testing of structured-metadata memory systems (e.g., MemOS-like designs, SSGM, ClawVM) against the attack catalog of earlier sections, to validate or refute the governance promises implicit in their architecture descriptions.

  5. R5.

    Benign-persistence benchmarks. Systematic evaluation of cross-user contamination, over-application of profile memory, context-integrity violations, and memory-induced sycophancy—treating these as primary security properties rather than usability concerns.

12.7. What This Agenda Is Not

We close this section with a caveat. An agenda of this kind risks implying that all open problems in the field can be resolved by assembling the listed directions. They cannot. Two classes of problems remain, in our view, genuinely unresolved and not reducible to any of the above.

First, the tension between audit retention and the right to forget is not a purely technical problem; it reflects a policy question about which state is audit-mandatory, which is operationally useful, and which is user-deletable (Section 9.4). Different jurisdictions and deployment contexts will resolve this tension differently, and no architectural primitive can substitute for that decision.

Second, the epistemic framing on which this survey rests—that memory is a mechanism for reconstructing a system’s operational past, and that its security protects a system’s authority over that past—is offered as a productive lens, not as a settled ontology. Alternative framings (purely capability-centric, or purely data-centric) could yield different agendas. We consider the framing productive if it leads to the primitives and questions we have articulated; we do not consider it privileged.

The research community’s task over the next few years will be to determine how many of these primitives and questions can be answered—and how many reveal, under investigation, deeper problems not yet named.

13. Conclusion

The long-term memory of LLM agents is transforming the security landscape in a way that is neither captured by classical data protection nor adequately addressed by existing prompt-injection literature. What has changed is not merely that agents now remember more; it is that memory has become a mechanism through which an agent’s past governs its future behavior. Once that happens, the center of security gravity shifts from is the current input harmful? to is the system’s memory state being poisoned, read without authorization, propagated across principals, or rendered irrecoverable?

This survey advanced three claims to respond to that shift.

Memory is inherently a security problem.

Cognitive neuroscience and the philosophy of memory portray human memory as reconstructive, reconsolidatable, externalizable, and socially contagious—precisely the properties that make LLM memory modules an independent class of security objects. The analogies we drew—source-monitoring failure as provenance failure, reconsolidation as read-time rewriting, social contagion as shared-memory contamination, confidence inflation as poisoned confidence calibration—are not decorative but load-bearing: each maps to a documented failure mode and a corresponding defense direction.

The memory lifecycle organizes the problem.

Organizing the literature along six phases (Write, Store, Retrieve, Execute, Share, Forget/Rollback) cross-tabulated with four objectives (integrity, confidentiality, availability, governance) exposed patterns that a flat, attack-name taxonomy obscures. The clearest such patterns were temporal decoupling (attacks introduced in one phase activate in another), compression-amplified promotion of toxins, the disproportionate contribution of internal channels to confidentiality failures, and the systematic under-development of Store and Forget/Rollback primitives in both research and deployed systems.

Mnemonic sovereignty names the normative goal.

Adapting the term from memory politics and the ethics of neurotechnology, we proposed mnemonic sovereignty as a system’s verifiable, recoverable governance over its own memory state. We then operationalized it via five testable primitives (write authorization, provenance visibility, principal-scoped retrieval, rollbackability, verified forgetting), each mapped to architectural substrates, representative threats, defense directions, and evaluation metrics. This framing is one of several possible; we consider it productive because it converts the high concept into research-tractable problems.

Against these claims we drew deliberately conservative conclusions about present capabilities. No published architecture fully implements the nine governance primitives required for lifecycle-wide sovereignty (Table 12). No published defense has been evaluated under adaptive LLM-driven red-teaming at the rigor established for prompt injection (Nasr et al., 2025). No peer-reviewed benchmark spans the full lifecycle and objective matrix under both adversarial and benign-persistence conditions. And the tension between audit retention and the right to forget remains unresolved at both the technical and the policy level.

The survey’s title, Security of Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents: Toward Mnemonic Sovereignty, reflects a deliberate choice of preposition. We did not claim that mnemonic sovereignty has been achieved, or even that its precise form is settled. We claimed that the field now needs the concept—and that the research agenda of the next several years will be measured, in large part, by how far it can move agents toward it. An agent that can be made to learn from its interactions but cannot reliably forget, that can be questioned but cannot be audited, that can remember but cannot be rolled back, is not a secure agent by any meaningful standard. The work of building agents that meet these standards has begun, but it remains substantial. A longer-term challenge looms beyond the current threat models: as agents increasingly write memories on behalf of other agents, memories will emerge from inter-agent interaction with no clear human authorization source—what we might call gray-zone memories. Attribution and accountability for such memories cannot be resolved by existing provenance mechanisms and will require fundamentally new governance abstractions.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
